lessons.title: Relations as typed facts
lessons.summary: Relations as typed facts, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
lessons.body:
In 1970 Edgar F. Codd, a researcher at IBM, published *A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks*. Many contemporary database interfaces were navigational: programs followed prescribed paths between records, coupling applications to access structures. Codd argued that applications should be insulated from representation changes.

Codd's idea was to describe data purely as **sets of facts**, with no pointers and no visible storage order. Programs say *what* they want, and the system works out *how* to fetch it. That separation, called **data independence**, is why you can add an index to a Postgres table today without touching a single query.

This lesson defines the vocabulary precisely. Every later lesson (algebra, dependencies, normal forms) builds on it.

## Relations, relational tuples and attributes

A **database relation** is a set of relational tuples that all share the same heading. Informally it is a table, but the precise definition matters.

```
Student
+-----+------+------+
| sid | name | year |   <- heading
+-----+------+------+
|  1  | Ada  |  2   |   <- relational tuple
|  2  | Ben  |  1   |
|  3  | Cat  |  2   |
+-----+------+------+
```

The drawing names the relation Student; its attributes are student id `sid`, student `name` and study `year`. This is the named-attribute presentation of the model: position in a printed table is a display choice. Codd’s original mathematical presentation used ordered domains; naming attributes avoids making that displayed order part of the meaning.

| Theory | SQL | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Relation | Table | A set of relational tuples |
| Tuple | Row | One fact |
| Attribute | Column | A named role |
| Domain | Type | Allowed values |

- The **relation heading** assigns each attribute name a domain. For example, `year` draws values from the integers one through four. A relational tuple assigns exactly one value from the correct domain to every attribute; a student name cannot occupy the year attribute.
- An **attribute domain** is the set of values an attribute may take. Codd required **atomic relational values**, indivisible from the database's point of view (more on that in the normal forms lesson).
- The **relation degree** (or arity) is the number of attributes: 3 above.
- The **cardinality** is the number of relational tuples: 3 above. It changes as rows are inserted; the degree does not.

### Each relational tuple is a true statement

The most useful way to read a relation is as a **relational predicate** with blanks:

> Student *sid* is called *name* and is in year *year*.

Every relational tuple fills in the blanks to make a true proposition. The relational tuple `(2, Ben, 1)` asserts "Student 2 is called Ben and is in year 1."

Under the **closed-world assumption**, the stored relation contains every true instance of its stated relational predicate. Only with that completeness assumption does an absent student relational tuple mean that the student does not exist in the population being modelled. SQL `NOT EXISTS` tests for returned rows regardless of whether the database is complete. A missing holiday booking can establish “no recorded holiday”; it cannot establish attendance, because illness and weekends are different facts.

```formula
r ⊆ D_sid × D_name × D_year
where
r: the finite set of Student relational tuples, shown in sid, name, year order for this card
D_sid: allowed student identifiers, here positive integers
D_name: allowed student names, here text strings
D_year: allowed study years, here integers one through four
⊆: is a subset of; every stored relational tuple must be a permitted combination
×: Cartesian product of domains, the set of all permitted value combinations
In words: The relation may contain only correctly typed combinations. Domains alone do not ensure that an identifier is unique; keys add that rule.
```

## Key takeaways

- A relational tuple assigns one correctly typed value to each named attribute.
- Degree counts attributes; cardinality counts relational tuples. Conclusions under the closed-world assumption require a complete relational predicate.

## Further reading

- [Codd: A Relational Model of Data (1970)](https://www.seas.upenn.edu/~zives/03f/cis550/codd.pdf)
- [PostgreSQL 18: constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html)
- [Reiter: On Closed World Data Bases](https://www.cs.ubc.ca/sites/default/files/tr/1977/TR-77-16.pdf)

questions.prompt: A relation `Course(cid, title, dept, credits)` currently holds 40 relational tuples. What are its degree and cardinality?

options.text: Degree 40, cardinality 4
options.explanation: Swapped. Degree counts attributes (columns); cardinality counts relational tuples (rows).

options.text: Degree 4, cardinality 40
options.explanation: Correct. There are 4 attributes in the heading, so the degree is 4. There are 40 relational tuples, so the cardinality is 40.

options.text: Degree 4, cardinality 4
options.explanation: This treats cardinality as fixed by the heading. Cardinality is the number of relational tuples and changes with every insert or delete.

options.text: Degree 1, cardinality 40
options.explanation: Degree is not the number of keys or relations; it is the number of attributes in the heading.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
degree(Course) = 4
|Course| = 40
where
degree: the number of attributes in a relation's heading (also called arity)
Course: the relation Course(cid, title, dept, credits)
| |: cardinality: the number of relational tuples in the relation inside the bars
In words: Course has 4 attributes (cid, title, dept, credits) and currently 40 relational tuples.
```

1. The heading is `{cid, title, dept, credits}`: 4 attributes, so the **degree is 4**.
2. The body has 40 relational tuples, so the **cardinality is 40**.
3. Insert another course and the cardinality becomes 41, while the degree stays 4. Schema changes such as adding or dropping a column change the degree; ordinary row inserts do not.

questions.prompt: A `holiday(employee_id, day)` relation lists booked days off. HR asks: "Was employee 42 working on 3 March?" There is no row `(42, '2026-03-03')`. A colleague argues the database cannot answer, because "absence of data is not data". Which reasoning matches how the relational model treats this?

options.text: The colleague is right; relational queries can only report facts that are present
options.explanation: Then `NOT EXISTS` and `EXCEPT` would be meaningless. The model deliberately lets absence carry meaning.

options.text: Under the closed-world assumption, the relation contains every true instance of its relational predicate, so a missing relational tuple means 'employee 42 had no holiday booked on 3 March' is true
options.explanation: Correct. The relational predicate is 'employee E has a holiday booked on day D'. The absent relational tuple makes that proposition false, so as long as the relational predicate is the full story the answer is that 42 was not on holiday.

options.text: The answer is NULL, because the fact is unknown
options.explanation: NULL is SQL’s marker for missing information within a row. A missing relational tuple is a different matter: under the stated completeness assumption, the booked-holiday relational predicate is false.

options.text: The database should be changed to store a row for every working day too
options.explanation: Storing working-day or attendance facts may be necessary to answer whether someone actually worked. It is unnecessary merely to answer whether a holiday booking exists. The two predicates are different.

questions.workedExample:
1. Write the relational predicate: *employee E has a holiday booked on day D*.
2. Closed-world assumption: the relation holds **all** true instances, so any (E, D) pair not present is false.
3. `(42, 2026-03-03)` is absent, so "42 had holiday booked on 3 March" is false.
4. In SQL:

```sql
SELECT NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM holiday
  WHERE employee_id = 42
    AND day = DATE '2026-03-03');
```

Caveat: this answers "not on holiday", not "was at work". Sickness lives in another relation, so the model only answers what its predicates cover.

lessons.title: Sets, bags and SQL results
lessons.summary: Sets, bags and SQL results, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
lessons.body:
## Consequences of "a set of relational tuples"

Because a relation is a mathematical set, three properties follow directly:

1. **No duplicate relational tuples.** Stating the same fact twice adds nothing. A set cannot contain an element twice.
2. **No relational tuple order.** Sets are unordered. "The first row" has no meaning; only `ORDER BY` imposes an order on a result.
3. **No attribute order.** The heading is a set too, so attributes are identified by name, not position.

> [!warning] SQL tables are not quite relations
> SQL is a pragmatic descendant of the model, and it deviates in ways that bite:
> - Tables and query results can be **bags** (multisets). Without a key, `INSERT` can add the same row twice, and `SELECT dept FROM emp` returns duplicates unless you write `DISTINCT`.
> - Columns have a position. `SELECT *` and `INSERT INTO t VALUES (...)` depend on it.
> - SQL has **NULL**, which the original model did not, giving three-valued logic.
> - Stored PostgreSQL row versions occupy physical locations, but those locations provide no guaranteed order in results. Postgres can return rows in a different order between two runs of the same query.

Chris Date and Hugh Darwen have criticised SQL’s duplicate rows and three-valued logic as departures from the relational model. In practice you get close to the model by giving every table a key and writing `DISTINCT` when you want a set.

## Common pitfalls

- **Tables without keys.** A log table with no primary key accumulates exact duplicates after a retried insert, and a predicate using only those stored attribute values cannot distinguish the copies; removing one may require a physical row identifier or a dialect-specific technique.
- **Relying on row order.** `SELECT ... LIMIT 1` without `ORDER BY` returns *some* row. It may change after a `VACUUM`, an index change or a parallel plan.
- **Mistaking current data for a rule.** Declaring `UNIQUE (name)` because today's names are unique will reject a legitimate insert later.
- **Pointers in disguise.** Storing `"row 5 of the other table"` or array positions as references reintroduces the navigational coupling Codd removed. Refer to rows by key value.

## Key takeaways

- Relations have neither duplicates nor intrinsic order; SQL can retain duplicates.
- Use deliberate duplicate removal and an ORDER BY with a unique tie-breaker when order matters.

## Further reading

- [Codd: A Relational Model of Data (1970)](https://www.seas.upenn.edu/~zives/03f/cis550/codd.pdf)
- [PostgreSQL 18: constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html)
- [Darwen: SQL language design and relational departures](https://www.dcs.warwick.ac.uk/~hugh/TTM/HAVING-A-Blunderful-Time.html)

questions.prompt: A query `SELECT * FROM orders LIMIT 10` returned rows in insertion order every time during testing. In production it suddenly returns a different set of 10 rows. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Relations have no relational tuple order, so without `ORDER BY` the database may return rows in any order it finds convenient
options.explanation: Correct. Insertion order was an accident of the physical layout. Updates, vacuuming, a new index or a parallel database scan can all change it. Only `ORDER BY` guarantees order.

options.text: Production has a bug in its storage engine
options.explanation: Nothing is wrong. Without `ORDER BY`, any order is a correct answer, so a different order is not a bug.

options.text: `LIMIT` always returns the most recently inserted rows
options.explanation: `LIMIT` takes the first N rows of whatever order the plan produces. It has no notion of recency.

options.text: Rows were deleted, which renumbered the table
options.explanation: Tables have no row numbers to renumber. References are by key value, not by position.

questions.workedExample:
1. A relation has no inherent row order. SQL results without `ORDER BY` likewise have unspecified order.
2. A convenient result sequence in testing is no guarantee. PostgreSQL may choose a different index, concurrent table-reading plan or storage access sequence.
3. An update can create a new PostgreSQL row version on the same page or another page; it need not move every updated row elsewhere.
4. Use `SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 10`, where `id` is unique, to break timestamp ties and select a determinate prefix.

questions.prompt: A `page_views(user_id, url, viewed_at)` table has no primary key or unique constraint. A retry bug inserts one row twice, exactly identical. What can you say about this table in relational terms?

options.text: It is still a relation; the two rows are different relational tuples because they were inserted at different times
options.explanation: Insertion time is not an attribute here. Two relational tuples with identical values for every attribute are the same relational tuple.

options.text: Nothing changes; queries automatically remove duplicates
options.explanation: Only `DISTINCT`, `UNION` (without `ALL`) and similar operators remove duplicates. `SELECT COUNT(*)` will count both rows.

options.text: The database will reject the second insert, because relations cannot hold duplicates
options.explanation: SQL permits duplicates unless a declared uniqueness rule or another explicit enforcement mechanism rejects them; it does not reject a retry merely because relational theory uses sets.

options.text: It is a bag, not a relation: it now contains a duplicate, which a set cannot, and with no key you cannot target just one copy with an ordinary `DELETE ... WHERE`
options.explanation: Correct. With no uniqueness constraint, exact duplicates can be stored. A value predicate matches both copies. PostgreSQL can distinguish current PostgreSQL row versions with its physical `ctid` column during cleanup, but that location is not a stable application identifier.

questions.workedExample:
1. Theory: a relation is a set of relational tuples, so a duplicate is impossible.
2. SQL tables are **bags**. With no key, nothing stops a duplicate.
3. `DELETE FROM page_views WHERE user_id = 7 AND url = '/a' AND viewed_at = '2026-03-03 09:00:00+00'` deletes **both** copies, because they are indistinguishable by value.
4. Remedies: add a key (for example a surrogate `id`, or `UNIQUE (user_id, url, viewed_at)` if that is a real rule), and make the insert idempotent with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are ways that SQL tables differ from relations as defined in the relational model? Select all that apply.

options.text: A table can contain duplicate rows
options.explanation: Correct. SQL tables and results are bags (multisets) unless a key or `DISTINCT` prevents duplicates.

options.text: Columns have an ordinal position that `SELECT *` and `INSERT ... VALUES` rely on
options.explanation: Correct. In the model, the heading is a set of named attributes, with no order.

options.text: A column can hold NULL, giving three-valued logic
options.explanation: Correct. The 1970 model had no NULL; SQL's NULL means a comparison can be *unknown*, not just true or false.

options.text: Every table must have a primary key
options.explanation: Wrong way round. The model requires every relation to have at least one candidate key; SQL does *not* require a key, which is exactly why duplicates are possible.

options.text: A table's attributes each have a type (domain)
options.explanation: This is shared, not a difference: the model's attributes each draw values from a domain, which SQL calls a type.

questions.workedExample:
Go through each property and ask "does the model allow this?"

1. Duplicates: a set cannot have them; a SQL table can. **Difference.**
2. Column order: a heading is a set; SQL columns are positional. **Difference.**
3. NULL: not in Codd's 1970 model; SQL has it. **Difference.**
4. Mandatory keys: the model implies every relation has a key (at worst all attributes). SQL lets you omit one. So this statement describes the model, not SQL.
5. Domains/types: present in both. **Not a difference.**

lessons.title: Choosing keys from legal states
lessons.summary: Choosing keys from legal states, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
lessons.body:
## Keys

A relation has no duplicate relational tuples, so the full set of attributes always identifies a relational tuple uniquely. Usually a smaller set does too.

- A **superkey** is any set of attributes whose values are unique across every relational tuple the relation could legally contain.
- A **candidate key** is a *minimal* superkey: remove any attribute and it stops being unique.
- The **primary key** is the candidate key you choose as the main way to identify relational tuples. The others are **alternate keys**, normally enforced in SQL with UNIQUE plus NOT NULL on their attributes.

Consider employees described by identifier `emp_id`, email address `email`, personal `name` and department `dept`. The domain guarantees that each identifier and each email belongs to only one employee:

| Attribute set | Superkey? | Candidate key? |
|---|---|---|
| identifier alone | Yes | Yes |
| email alone | Yes | Yes |
| identifier and name together | Yes | No, not minimal |
| name and department together | No | No |

> [!tip] Keys are about rules, not current data
> A key is a claim about *every legal state* of the relation, not the rows you happen to have. If today no two employees share a name, the name alone is still not a key, because the business allows two people called Sam. Keys come from the domain, and you find them by asking "can this ever repeat?"

## Key takeaways

- A candidate key is a superkey minimal under inclusion.
- Choose keys from rules for every legal state, not uniqueness in a sample.

## Further reading

- [Codd: A Relational Model of Data (1970)](https://www.seas.upenn.edu/~zives/03f/cis550/codd.pdf)
- [PostgreSQL 18: constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html)

questions.prompt: In `Employee(emp_id, email, name, dept)`, both `emp_id` and `email` are unique for every employee the business could ever have. Which statement is correct?

options.text: `{emp_id, email}` is a candidate key because it contains both unique columns
options.explanation: It is a superkey, but not minimal: dropping either attribute leaves a set that is still unique. A candidate key must be minimal.

options.text: Only the primary key can be a candidate key
options.explanation: Backwards. The primary key is chosen *from* the candidate keys; a relation can have several candidate keys.

options.text: `{emp_id}` and `{email}` are both candidate keys; one is chosen as primary key and the other becomes an alternate key
options.explanation: Correct. Each is unique and minimal (a single attribute cannot be reduced). Pick one as primary key and enforce the other with `UNIQUE`.

options.text: `{emp_id, name}` is a candidate key because names help identify people
options.explanation: Adding `name` to a key makes a superkey that is not minimal. Usefulness to humans is not part of the definition.

questions.workedExample:
Check each set against the two conditions for a candidate key:

| Set | Unique? | Minimal? |
|---|---|---|
| `{emp_id}` | Yes | Yes |
| `{email}` | Yes | Yes |
| `{emp_id, email}` | Yes | No |
| `{emp_id, name}` | Yes | No |

So there are two candidate keys. In SQL:

PostgreSQL column declarations (inside a CREATE TABLE statement):

```sql
emp_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
email  TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
```

questions.prompt: A designer looks at 5,000 rows in `customer(name, postcode, phone)`, sees that no two rows share a `(name, postcode)` pair, and declares it the primary key. What is the main flaw?

options.text: A key is a rule about every legal state of the relation, not a pattern in today's rows; two customers with the same name can live in the same postcode
options.explanation: Correct. Uniqueness in a sample proves nothing about the future. Two J. Smiths in one postcode is perfectly legal, so the second one's insert would be wrongly rejected.

options.text: Keys must be chosen from integer columns
options.explanation: Keys need not be integers: text, UUID and date columns can be used, and a key can span several columns.

options.text: Composite primary keys are not allowed
options.explanation: They are allowed and common, for example `PRIMARY KEY (sid, cid)` on a link table.

options.text: `phone` should have been included to make it minimal
options.explanation: Adding attributes makes a key less minimal, not more, and phone numbers are shared and change too.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ask the domain question: *can two different customers ever have the same name and postcode?* Yes: families, flats, common names.
2. So `{name, postcode}` is not a superkey of the relation's legal states, whatever the current data shows.
3. A postcode can be shared by multiple addresses, so it cannot uniquely identify a customer.
4. Better: a surrogate `customer_id`, plus `UNIQUE` only on attributes the business guarantees are unique (perhaps an email used for login).

lessons.title: Enforcing relational integrity
lessons.summary: Enforcing relational integrity, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
lessons.body:
## Foreign keys

A **foreign key** is a set of attributes in one relation whose values must appear as a key in another (or the same) relation.

An enrolment carries student id `sid` and course code `cid`. Its student id refers by value to the key of Student, and its course code to the key of Course.

The arrows say that every `sid` in `Enrolled` must be the `sid` of some existing student. Foreign keys are how relations refer to each other without pointers: the reference is a *value*, matched at query time by a join.

## Integrity rules

The model comes with constraints that every database state must satisfy.

1. **Entity integrity**: no attribute of a primary key may be NULL. A fact about "a student whose id is unknown" cannot be identified, so it cannot be referred to.
2. **Referential integrity**: in the null-free theory, a foreign key must match a referenced key value. SQL adds nullable references. PostgreSQL’s default `MATCH SIMPLE` waives a composite reference when any referencing column is NULL; `MATCH FULL` permits a reference with all columns NULL but rejects a mixture of NULL and non-NULL. Use `NOT NULL` on every referencing column when participation is mandatory.
3. **relational domain constraints**: values come from the attribute's domain (`year` is an integer from 1 to 4, say).
4. **Relational key constraints**: no two relational tuples agree on a candidate key.

In PostgreSQL these map to DDL (create the referenced course table first). SQLite ordinary rowid tables have a historical exception allowing NULL in some declared primary keys; use explicit NOT NULL, STRICT or WITHOUT ROWID as appropriate:

```sql
-- Referenced keys must exist first.
CREATE TABLE course (
  cid TEXT PRIMARY KEY
);

CREATE TABLE student (
  sid   INT PRIMARY KEY,
  email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name  TEXT NOT NULL,
  year  INT NOT NULL
    CHECK (year BETWEEN 1 AND 4)
);

CREATE TABLE enrolled (
  sid INT REFERENCES student(sid),
  cid TEXT REFERENCES course(cid),
  PRIMARY KEY (sid, cid)
);
```

The composite primary key on `enrolled` does two jobs. It identifies each enrolment, and it stops the same student enrolling on the same course twice.

When a referenced row is deleted, the foreign key's `ON DELETE` action decides what happens: `NO ACTION` (the PostgreSQL default, with checking deferrable if declared so), `RESTRICT` (reject immediately, without deferring), `CASCADE` (delete the referencing rows), `SET NULL` or `SET DEFAULT`.

A PostgreSQL `UNIQUE` constraint alone allows multiple NULLs by default. Use `UNIQUE` together with `NOT NULL` for a conventional alternate key. `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` changes uniqueness treatment, but still permits a missing value and is not a replacement for `NOT NULL`. A `CHECK` accepts true or unknown, so a domain range check by itself does not forbid NULL.

## Key takeaways

- Keys, domain rules and references constrain which database states are legal.
- PostgreSQL CHECK, nullable UNIQUE and nullable foreign keys need explicit NULL decisions.

## Further reading

- [Codd: A Relational Model of Data (1970)](https://www.seas.upenn.edu/~zives/03f/cis550/codd.pdf)
- [PostgreSQL 18: constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html)

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, `enrolled(sid, cid)` has primary key `(sid, cid)`, a foreign key from `sid` to `student.sid` and another from `cid` to `course.cid`, both with the default `ON DELETE` action. You run `DELETE FROM student WHERE sid = 3;` while student 3 has two enrolments. What happens?

options.text: The student and both enrolments are deleted
options.explanation: That would be `ON DELETE CASCADE`, which must be asked for explicitly. It is not the default.

options.text: The student is deleted and the two enrolments get `sid = NULL`
options.explanation: That is `ON DELETE SET NULL`. It would also fail here, because `sid` is part of the primary key and so cannot be NULL.

options.text: The delete fails with a foreign-key violation, because the default foreign-key action (`NO ACTION`) forbids leaving enrolments that reference a missing student
options.explanation: Correct. The default checks referential integrity and raises an error if referencing rows remain. Delete the enrolments first, or declare `ON DELETE CASCADE`.

options.text: The student is deleted and the enrolments are left pointing at nothing
options.explanation: Referential integrity exists precisely to prevent references to absent database rows; the database will not allow this state.

questions.workedExample:
1. Referential integrity: every `Enrolled.sid` must match an existing `Student.sid`.
2. Deleting student 3 would leave two enrolments with `sid = 3` and no matching student.
3. The default `ON DELETE NO ACTION` checks this (at the end of the statement, or at commit if the constraint is deferred) and raises `violates foreign relational key constraint`.
4. Options:
   - `ON DELETE CASCADE`: removes the enrolments automatically.
   - Delete from `enrolled` first, in the same transaction.
   - `SET NULL` is impossible here because `sid` is in the primary key (entity integrity).

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, you are reviewing `CREATE TABLE enrolled (sid INT REFERENCES student, cid TEXT REFERENCES course, grade TEXT);` Which changes enforce rules that the relational model expects of this relation? Select all that apply.

options.text: `PRIMARY KEY (sid, cid)`
options.explanation: Correct. It gives the relation a candidate key, rules out duplicate enrolments, and, through entity integrity, makes `sid` and `cid` NOT NULL.

options.text: `CHECK (grade IN ('A','B','C','D','E','F'))`
options.explanation: Correct. This CHECK limits non-NULL grades to A–F. Add NOT NULL as well if missing grades are forbidden; a CHECK accepts UNKNOWN.

options.text: An index on `grade` to speed up grade reports
options.explanation: An index is a physical design decision. It changes performance, not which states are legal.

options.text: Making `sid` the first column so it is easier to join
options.explanation: Column position has no meaning in the model, and join performance does not depend on column order.

questions.workedExample:
Sort the proposals into *logical rules* and *physical tuning*:

| Change | Kind | Model rule |
|---|---|---|
| PK (sid, cid) | logical | key + entity integrity |
| CHECK grade | logical | domain |
| index on grade | physical | none |
| column order | neither | attributes unordered |

Note that a primary key implies `NOT NULL` on its columns in PostgreSQL, which is entity integrity in action.

lessons.title: Data independence and query interfaces
lessons.summary: Data independence and query interfaces, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
lessons.body:
## Why the model won

The navigational databases of the 1960s, such as IBM's IMS (hierarchical) and CODASYL (network) systems, were fast for the access paths they were built for, and painful for everything else. The relational model made three goals central to its interface.

- **Physical data independence.** Indexes, partitioning and storage format can change without changing queries.
- **Logical data independence.** Views let you restructure tables while keeping old queries working.
- **Declarative queries.** Because queries are expressed over sets with well-defined operators (the next lesson), an optimiser can rewrite them into equivalent, cheaper forms.

The doubt in the 1970s was whether a declarative system could ever be fast enough. IBM's System R and Berkeley's Ingres answered that by the late 1970s; System R also produced SQL and a pioneering cost-based optimiser. Oracle, DB2, Postgres (a descendant of Ingres research) and SQLite all follow.

> [!note] NULL, briefly
> SQL uses NULL to represent missing information. Comparisons with NULL yield *unknown*, so `WHERE x = NULL` matches nothing, and `NOT IN` against a list that contains a NULL returns no rows. The SQL fundamentals module covers the details. For theory, the key point is that NULL breaks the clean "each relational tuple is a true proposition" reading, which is one reason designers try to minimise nullable columns.

## Key takeaways

- Physical data independence isolates applications from storage choices.
- Logical data independence can preserve a query interface through views while tables change.

## Further reading

- [Codd: A Relational Model of Data (1970)](https://www.seas.upenn.edu/~zives/03f/cis550/codd.pdf)
- [PostgreSQL 18: constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html)

questions.prompt: A view `active_students` is defined as `SELECT sid, name FROM student WHERE status = 'active'`. The team later splits `student` into two tables and redefines the view over them, and the reporting queries keep working unchanged. Which property of the relational model does this demonstrate?

options.text: Physical data independence
options.explanation: Physical data independence covers storage changes, such as adding an index or changing file layout. Splitting a table is a change to the logical schema.

options.text: The closed-world assumption
options.explanation: That assumption says absent relational tuples are false. It does not explain why queries survived a schema change.

options.text: Referential integrity
options.explanation: Referential integrity is about foreign key values matching keys. Nothing here involves foreign keys.

options.text: Logical data independence
options.explanation: Correct. The logical schema (the tables) changed, but the external schema the reports use (the view) stayed the same, so applications were insulated from the change.

questions.workedExample:
There are three levels in the classic architecture:

lessons.title: Restrict, project and rename
lessons.summary: Restrict, project and rename, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
lessons.body:
Relational algebra is a small set of operators that each take one or two relations and return a new relation. That last part is the whole trick: because the output is always a relation, you can feed it into another operator, and build any query expressible in ordinary relational algebra by **composing** a few simple pieces.

You never type relational algebra into Postgres. But the database translates your SQL into a tree of algebra-like operators, transforms that tree into a cheaper equivalent, and then executes it. An `EXPLAIN` plan shows physical implementations of algebra-like operations, along with SQL extensions such as sorting and aggregation.

Each operator has a one-character symbol, mostly Greek letters. Every symbol is explained in the formula card where it first appears, and again in each card that uses it, so you can read any card on its own.

## Local relations

```
Student            Enrolled     Course
sid name year      sid cid      cid dept
 1  Ada   2         1  DB       DB  CS
 2  Ben   1         1  OS       OS  CS
 3  Cat   2         1  LA       LA  MA
 4  Dev   3         2  DB
                    3  DB
                    3  OS
```

Four students, three courses, six enrolments. Dev is not enrolled on anything. (Course also has a `title` column, left out here for width.) `sid` is the student id, `cid` the course code, and `dept` the department that runs the course.

## Unary operators: selection, projection and rename

A unary operator takes one relation as input. There are three.

**Selection (σ)** keeps the relational tuples that satisfy a condition. It filters *rows*. It is written σ, the Greek letter sigma, followed by the condition and then the input relation in brackets:

```formula
σ year=2 (Student)
where
σ: selection (the Greek letter sigma): keep only the relational tuples for which the condition written straight after it is true
year: the attribute of Student holding the student's year of study, an integer from 1 to 4
Student: the relation of students, with attributes sid, name and year (four relational tuples in the running example)
In words: from Student, keep just the students who are in year 2.
```

```
sid name year
 1  Ada   2
 3  Cat   2
```

The result has the same attributes as the input; only rows have gone.

**Projection (π)** keeps only the named attributes. It chooses *columns*, and because the result is a set, duplicates disappear. It is written with the Greek letter π (pi), followed by the attributes to keep:

```formula
π cid (Enrolled) = {DB, OS, LA}
where
π: projection (the Greek letter pi; here it has nothing to do with the circle constant 3.14159): keep only the attributes listed straight after it, then remove any duplicate relational tuples
cid: the course-code attribute
Enrolled: the relation recording which student is enrolled on which course, with attributes sid and cid (six relational tuples in the running example)
{ }: a set: a collection of distinct values, with no order
DB, OS, LA: the three course codes in the running example
In words: list the course codes that appear in Enrolled, each once.
```

Six enrolments, but only three relational tuples in the result. SQL's `SELECT cid FROM enrolled` returns six rows; you need `SELECT DISTINCT cid` to match the algebra.

**Rename (ρ)** changes a relation's or an attribute's name. It is written with the Greek letter ρ (rho), in one of two forms:

```formula
ρ S (R)
ρ b←a (R)
where
ρ: rename (the Greek letter rho): give the input a new name without changing its relational tuples
R: the input relation
S: the new name for the whole relation, in the first form
a: an attribute's current name, in the second form
b: the new name for attribute a
←: "takes the place of": the name on the left replaces the name on the right
In words: the first form calls relation R by the new name S; the second keeps the relation but renames its attribute a to b.
```

For a self-join, make the two headings distinct before a Cartesian product. Here we use qualified names as shorthand for renaming every attribute in each copy: the first has `S1.sid`, `S1.name`, `S1.year`; the second has the corresponding `S2` names. Merely giving a relation a new label is insufficient in a strictly named-attribute algebra.

> [!note] Name clash: σ is not SELECT
> SQL's `SELECT` list is a **projection (π)**. The selection σ corresponds to `WHERE`. The names are a historical accident that confuses almost everyone once.

```formula
σ S1.year=S2.year ∧ S1.sid<S2.sid
  (ρ S1 (Student) × ρ S2 (Student))
where
Student: the four local student relational tuples
ρ: qualify every attribute with the following copy name
S1, S2: the two disjointly named copies
S1.year, S2.year: each copy’s study-year attribute
S1.sid, S2.sid: each copy’s student-id attribute
σ: keep only relational tuples satisfying the predicate
∧: both conditions must hold
<: less than
×: Cartesian product, every pair of students
In words: There are sixteen pairs before filtering. Equal years leave six pairs; increasing student id removes self-pairs and reverse copies, leaving Ada with Cat once.
```

## Key takeaways

- Selection keeps rows; projection keeps attributes and removes duplicate relational tuples.
- Give self-join copies distinct attribute names before forming a product.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational model and algebra](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch2.pdf)
- [PostgreSQL 18: constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html)

lessons.title: Set operators and an algebraic basis
lessons.summary: Set operators and an algebraic basis, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
lessons.body:
## Local relations

```
Student            Enrolled     Course
sid name year      sid cid      cid dept
 1  Ada   2         1  DB       DB  CS
 2  Ben   1         1  OS       OS  CS
 3  Cat   2         1  LA       LA  MA
 4  Dev   3         2  DB
                    3  DB
                    3  OS
```

Four students, three courses, six enrolments. Dev is not enrolled on anything. (Course also has a `title` column, left out here for width.) `sid` is the student id, `cid` the course code, and `dept` the department that runs the course.

## Set operators: union, difference, intersection

Union, difference and intersection work as they do on any sets, with one rule: the two inputs must be **union-compatible**, meaning the same attributes with the same domains.

```formula
R ∪ S
R − S
R ∩ S
where
R, S: two union-compatible relations (same attribute names, same domains)
∪: union: every relational tuple that is in R, in S, or in both, listed once
−: difference: the relational tuples of R that are not in S. Order matters: R − S is not the same as S − R
∩: intersection: the relational tuples that are in both R and S
In words: union combines two relations, difference removes one from the other, and intersection keeps what they share.
```

Students who are not enrolled on anything:

```formula
π sid (Student) − π sid (Enrolled)
{1, 2, 3, 4} − {1, 2, 3} = {4}
where
π: projection: keep only the listed attribute, removing duplicates
sid: the student-id attribute, present in both Student and Enrolled
Student: the relation of students (sid, name, year)
Enrolled: the relation of enrolments (sid, cid)
−: difference: the values on the left that are not on the right
{ }: a set of distinct values
In words: take every student id, remove the ids that appear in Enrolled, and only Dev (id 4) is left.
```

Students taking both DB and course labelled OS:

```formula
π sid (σ cid='DB' (Enrolled))
  ∩ π sid (σ cid='OS' (Enrolled))
{1, 2, 3} ∩ {1, 3} = {1, 3}
where
σ: selection: keep the relational tuples where the condition is true; here cid='DB' keeps enrolments on the course with code DB (quoted values are literal text)
π: projection: keep only the listed attribute, removing duplicates
sid: the student-id attribute
cid: the course-code attribute
Enrolled: the relation of enrolments (sid, cid)
∩: intersection: the values that appear on both sides
{ }: a set of distinct values
In words: the students on DB are 1, 2 and 3; those on course labelled OS are 1 and 3; the students on both are 1 and 3 (Ada and Cat).
```

In SQL these are `UNION`, `EXCEPT` and `INTERSECT`, which remove duplicates by default; `UNION ALL` and friends keep them (bag semantics).

## The six primitive operators

Six operators are enough to express everything else: selection σ, projection π, rename ρ, union ∪, difference − and Cartesian product ×. The rest are shorthand:

```formula
R ⋈θ S = σθ (R × S)
R ∩ S = R − (R − S)
R ⋉ S = π A_R (R ⋈ S)
where
R, S: relations with disjoint headings for the theta-join line, union-compatible headings for the intersection line, and compatible shared domains for the natural semijoin line
⋈θ: theta join with condition θ; a bare ⋈ is the natural join
θ: theta, the join condition
σ: selection: keep relational tuples where a condition holds
×: Cartesian product: every pairing of a relational tuple of R with a relational tuple of S
∩: intersection: relational tuples in both R and S
−: difference: relational tuples in the left input but not the right
⋉: semijoin: the relational tuples of R with at least one match in S
π: projection: keep only the listed attributes
A_R: the list of R's attributes
In words: a join is a product then a selection; the intersection is "R minus the part of R that is not in S"; a semijoin is a join cut back to R's columns.
```

Check the intersection rule on small sets of numbers:

```formula
R = {1, 2, 3} and S = {2, 3, 4}
R − S = {1}
R − (R − S) = {2, 3} = R ∩ S
where
R, S: two small example sets
{ }: a set of distinct values
−: difference: what is in the left set but not the right
∩: intersection: what is in both
In words: removing from R the part that is not in S leaves exactly what R and S share.
```

Division is also derived; the neighbouring division unit works through its construction.

This is a conventional complete basis of six operators, rather than a claim that every presentation uses this exact primitive list. A language expressing all pure-algebra queries is **relationally complete**. SQL can express them using appropriate duplicate removal and null-free inputs, and adds ordering, aggregation and recursion.

## Key takeaways

- Union, difference and intersection require compatible headings and domains.
- “On course labelled OS but not LA” needs a difference between student sets, not a contradictory row predicate.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational model and algebra](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch2.pdf)
- [PostgreSQL 18: constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html)

options.text: × (Cartesian product)
options.explanation: Correct. Product is primitive; every join is defined as a product followed by a selection.

options.text: − (difference)
options.explanation: Correct. Difference is primitive, and intersection is derived from it: the intersection of R and S is R minus the part of R that is not in S.

options.text: ⋈ (natural join)
options.explanation: Derived: it is a product, a selection on equal shared attributes, and a projection to drop the duplicate columns.

options.explanation: Derived from difference: R minus (R minus S). A common mistake is to assume all three set operators are primitive.

lessons.title: Products and joins
lessons.summary: Products and joins, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
lessons.body:
## Local relations

```
Student            Enrolled     Course
sid name year      sid cid      cid dept
 1  Ada   2         1  DB       DB  CS
 2  Ben   1         1  OS       OS  CS
 3  Cat   2         1  LA       LA  MA
 4  Dev   3         2  DB
                    3  DB
                    3  OS
```

Four students, three courses, six enrolments. Dev is not enrolled on anything. (Course also has a `title` column, left out here for width.) `sid` is the student id, `cid` the course code, and `dept` the department that runs the course.

## Product and joins

The **Cartesian product** pairs every relational tuple of one relation with every relational tuple of another, so its size is the product of the two sizes:

```formula
|R × S| = |R| × |S|
|Student × Course| = 4 × 3 = 12
where
R, S: two relations with disjoint attribute names, renaming first if necessary
× (between relations): the Cartesian product: one output relational tuple for every pairing of a relational tuple of R with a relational tuple of S, carrying the attributes of both
× (between numbers): ordinary multiplication
| |: the cardinality of the relation inside the bars: its number of relational tuples
Student: the relation of students, 4 relational tuples
Course: the relation of courses, 3 relational tuples
In words: pairing 4 students with 3 courses in every possible way gives 12 relational tuples.
```

On its own the product is rarely what you want; it is the raw material for joins.

A **theta join** is a product followed by a selection:

```formula
R ⋈θ S ≡ σθ (R × S)
where
R, S: two relations with disjoint attribute names, renaming first if necessary
⋈: join (the "bow-tie" symbol): combine relational tuples of R and S that satisfy a condition
θ: theta, the join condition written under or after the bow-tie, such as R.a = S.b or R.a < S.b
σ: selection: keep only the relational tuples for which a condition is true
×: the Cartesian product: every relational tuple of R paired with every relational tuple of S
≡: is equivalent to: always gives exactly the same result
In words: a theta join is "pair everything, then keep the pairs that satisfy θ". This defines the result, not a required execution algorithm. A database can avoid enumerating rejected pairs with an index or hash join; a cross join or some nested-loop plans can still enumerate every pair.
```

When θ uses only equality it is an **equijoin**. A **natural join**, written with a bare bow-tie and no condition, is the equijoin on *all* attributes with the same name, keeping one copy of each:

```formula
Student ⋈ Enrolled
where
⋈: natural join (a bow-tie with no condition): pair the relational tuples that have equal values on every attribute name the two relations share, and keep one copy of each shared attribute
Student: the relation (sid, name, year)
Enrolled: the relation (sid, cid); the only shared attribute name is sid
In words: attach to each student the courses they are enrolled on, matching on sid.
```

```
sid name year cid
 1  Ada   2   DB
 1  Ada   2   OS
 1  Ada   2   LA
 2  Ben   1   DB
 3  Cat   2   DB
 3  Cat   2   OS
```

Dev vanishes: an inner join keeps only relational tuples with a partner. The extended algebra adds **outer joins**, which keep unmatched relational tuples padded with NULLs, plus the **semijoin** and **antijoin**, which optimisers use constantly:

```formula
R ⟕ S
R ⟖ S
R ⟗ S
R ⋉ S
R ▷ S
where
R, S: two relations with compatible shared domains; these bare symbols use natural matching on shared attribute names
⟕: left outer join: the join, plus every relational tuple of R with no partner, padded with NULL for S's attributes
⟖: right outer join: the same, keeping unmatched relational tuples of S instead
⟗: full outer join: keeps unmatched relational tuples from both sides
⋉: semijoin: the relational tuples of R that have at least one match in S, with R's attributes only
▷: antijoin: the relational tuples of R that have no match in S
In words: outer joins keep the rows a join would drop; semijoin asks "does a match exist?" and antijoin asks "is there no match?".
```

- **Semijoin** R ⋉ S is SQL's `WHERE EXISTS`.
- **Antijoin** R ▷ S is SQL's `WHERE NOT EXISTS`.
- **Left outer join** R ⟕ S is SQL's `LEFT JOIN`.

> [!warning] Natural join is fragile
> Natural join matches on every shared column name. If someone later adds `updated_at` to both Student and Enrolled, `NATURAL JOIN` silently starts requiring equal timestamps and returns almost nothing. Production SQL should spell out `JOIN ... ON` or `USING (sid)`.

For a natural join, shared attribute names must have compatible domains. With no shared names, the matching condition is vacuously true, and the result is the Cartesian product: four students paired with three courses give twelve relational tuples. Adding a same-named column later changes a SQL `NATURAL JOIN` predicate, so explicit join conditions are safer in application SQL. The outer-join operators above belong to an extension with missing-value markers, rather than the null-free algebra.

## Key takeaways

- A product contains every pair; a theta join retains pairs satisfying its predicate.
- Natural joins match all shared names; outer joins preserve unmatched rows with missing-value markers.

lessons.summary: Division and universal conditions, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
lessons.body:
## Local relations

```
Student            Enrolled     Course
sid name year      sid cid      cid dept
 1  Ada   2         1  DB       DB  CS
 2  Ben   1         1  OS       OS  CS
 3  Cat   2         1  LA       LA  MA
 4  Dev   3         2  DB
                    3  DB
                    3  OS
```

Four students, three courses, six enrolments. Dev is not enrolled on anything. (Course also has a `title` column, left out here for width.) `sid` is the student id, `cid` the course code, and `dept` the department that runs the course.

## Division: "for all"

Division answers questions with *every* in them: which students take **all** CS courses?

```formula
Enrolled ÷ π cid (σ dept='CS' (Course))
  = {1, 3}
where
÷: division: the values of the left relation's remaining attributes (here sid) that are paired, in the left relation, with every relational tuple of the right relation
Enrolled: the relation of enrolments (sid, cid)
π: projection: keep only the listed attribute, removing duplicates
cid: the course-code attribute
σ: selection: keep relational tuples where the condition holds; dept='CS' keeps courses run by the CS department
dept: the attribute of Course naming the department
Course: the relation of courses (cid, title, dept)
{ }: a set of distinct values
In words: the divisor relation is the set of CS courses, {DB, course labelled OS}; the result is every student id enrolled on all of them.
```

A student qualifies if, for every course in the divisor relation, the pair (student, course) appears in Enrolled. Ada (1) and Cat (3) take both; Ben takes only DB. Result: `{1, 3}`.

Division is derived from the basic operators, which shows how "for all" becomes "there is no counterexample":

```formula
A = π sid (Enrolled) = {1, 2, 3}
B = π cid (σ dept='CS' (Course))
B = {DB, OS}
M = (A × B) − Enrolled = {(2, OS)}
Enrolled ÷ B = A − π sid (M)
Enrolled ÷ B = {1, 2, 3} − {2} = {1, 3}
where
A: every student id that has at least one enrolment (the candidates)
B: the divisor relation: the CS course codes
M: the missing pairs: every (student, CS course) pair that should exist if everyone took everything, minus the pairs that do exist
π: projection: keep only the listed attribute, removing duplicates
σ: selection: keep relational tuples where the condition holds
×: Cartesian product: every pairing of a value of A with a value of B
−: difference: what is on the left but not on the right
÷: division, as defined above
sid, cid, dept: the student-id, course-code and department attributes
DB, OS: the codes of the two CS courses
Enrolled, Course: the relations of the running example
{ }: a set; (2, course labelled OS) is one pair, a relational tuple of student 2 and course course labelled OS
In words: list every pair that "taking all CS courses" would need, find the pairs that are missing, and remove any student with a missing pair. Ben (2) is missing course labelled OS, so only Ada and Cat remain.
```

SQL has no division operator. The standard idiom is a double `NOT EXISTS`: there is no CS course that the student is not enrolled on.

```sql
SELECT s.sid FROM student s
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM course c
  WHERE c.dept = 'CS'
    AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM enrolled e
      WHERE e.sid = s.sid
        AND e.cid = c.cid));
```

> [!example] The empty divisor relation
> If the CS department had no courses, the inner condition is vacuously true, and the SQL above returns **every** student, including Dev. The algebraic version returns only the students in A, those with at least one enrolment. Both are logically defensible ("all of nothing" is true), but they differ. Decide which you intend before shipping a "customers who bought every item in the promotional bundle" report.

## Key takeaways

- Division removes candidates with any missing required pair.
- An empty divisor qualifies every candidate; choose whether candidates come from enrolments or all students.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational model and algebra](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch2.pdf)
- [PostgreSQL 18: constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html)

lessons.title: Equivalent query plans
lessons.summary: Equivalent query plans, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
lessons.body:
## Local relations

```
Student            Enrolled     Course
sid name year      sid cid      cid dept
 1  Ada   2         1  DB       DB  CS
 2  Ben   1         1  OS       OS  CS
 3  Cat   2         1  LA       LA  MA
 4  Dev   3         2  DB
                    3  DB
                    3  OS
```

Four students, three courses, six enrolments. Dev is not enrolled on anything. (Course also has a `title` column, left out here for width.) `sid` is the student id, `cid` the course code, and `dept` the department that runs the course.

## From SQL to an expression tree

A simple SQL block maps onto algebra almost mechanically:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT s.name
FROM student s JOIN enrolled e
  ON s.sid = e.sid
WHERE e.cid = 'DB';
```

Written as one algebra expression, read from the inside out:

```formula
π name (σ cid='DB' (Student ⋈ Enrolled))
where
π: projection: keep only the listed attribute, removing duplicates (SQL's SELECT DISTINCT)
name: the student-name attribute
σ: selection: keep relational tuples where the condition holds (SQL's WHERE)
cid: the course-code attribute
⋈: natural join: pair relational tuples with equal values on the shared attribute, here sid (SQL's JOIN ... ON s.sid = e.sid)
Student, Enrolled: the relations of the running example
In words: join students to their enrolments, keep the DB enrolments, then list the distinct names.
```

The same expression as a tree, with S for Student and E for Enrolled:

```
π name
  |
σ cid='DB'
  |
  ⋈ sid
 / \
S   E
```

Read from the bottom up: join, filter, project. The result is `{Ada, Ben, Cat}`.

## Equivalences: why optimisers work

Because operators have precise meanings, there are rules that transform one expression into another that is guaranteed to give the same result. Four of the most important:

1. **Cascade selections**: a selection on two conditions joined by "and" is the same as two selections, one after the other.
2. **Commute joins**: the order of a join's inputs does not matter, and joins are associative, so join order is free to choose.
3. **Push selection below a join**: if a condition mentions only one input's attributes, filter that input before joining.
4. **Push projection down**: drop columns early, keeping any needed by later joins or filters.

```formula
σ p∧q (R) ≡ σ p (σ q (R))
R ⋈ S ≡ S ⋈ R
(R ⋈ S) ⋈ T ≡ R ⋈ (S ⋈ T)
σ p (R ⋈ S) ≡ σ p (R) ⋈ S
π L (R ⋈ S)
  ≡ π L (π L_R (R) ⋈ π L_S (S))
where
R, S, T: any relations
σ: selection: keep relational tuples where the condition holds
p, q: conditions on attributes. In the fourth line, p must mention only R's attributes
∧: and: both conditions must be true
⋈: natural join
≡: is equivalent to: gives exactly the same result for every possible contents of R, S and T
π: projection: keep only the listed attributes
L: the attributes the final result needs
L_R, L_S: the attributes of R (and of S) that are in L or are needed for the join
In words: line 1 is rule 1, lines 2 and 3 are rule 2, line 4 is rule 3 and the last line is rule 4.
```

Rule 3 is the big one. Take the tree above with 10,000 students and 200,000 enrolments, 1,000 of them for DB:

```
naive:   join 10k with 200k
         -> 200k rows, then filter -> 1k
pushed:  filter E first -> 1k rows
         join 10k with 1k -> 1k rows
```

The pushed plan feeds 1,000 enrolments into the join instead of 200,000. Every cost-based optimiser (Postgres, SQL Server, Oracle, the Spark SQL Catalyst optimiser) applies these algebraic rewrites, then uses statistics to choose among the equivalent trees. The query processing module covers how it picks.

## Key takeaways

- Rewrites must preserve values, multiplicities and the output heading under the intended semantics.
- Push one-input filters below inner joins and keep needed join and output attributes.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational model and algebra](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch2.pdf)
- [PostgreSQL 18: constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html)

```formula
>: greater than
```

```formula
o.total: order total, in the same currency as the limit
In words: Attempt to test the full two-input condition on Customer alone. Customer has no order total, so this is not well typed.
```
options.explanation: Customer has no `total` attribute; only predicates over one relation's attributes can be pushed to it.

options.text: No rewrite is valid, because the predicate mentions both relations
options.explanation: The conjunction can be split (a selection on "p and q" equals a selection on p followed by one on q), and the part that mentions only Customer can then be pushed.

```formula
σ p∧q (X) ≡ σ q (σ p (X))
σ p (C ⋈ O) ≡ σ p (C) ⋈ O
σ q (σ p (Customer) ⋈ Order)
where
σ: selection: keep relational tuples where the condition is true
```

lessons.title: Where pure algebra stops
lessons.summary: Where pure algebra stops, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
lessons.body:
## Local relations

```
Student            Enrolled     Course
sid name year      sid cid      cid dept
 1  Ada   2         1  DB       DB  CS
 2  Ben   1         1  OS       OS  CS
 3  Cat   2         1  LA       LA  MA
 4  Dev   3         2  DB
                    3  DB
                    3  OS
```

Four students, three courses, six enrolments. Dev is not enrolled on anything. (Course also has a `title` column, left out here for width.) `sid` is the student id, `cid` the course code, and `dept` the department that runs the course.

## Pitfalls and limits

- **Bags versus sets.** SQL works on bags, so some algebraic equivalences need care. For sets, a relation unioned with itself is unchanged; in SQL, `R UNION ALL R` has twice as many rows. An optimiser may only apply a rewrite if it holds under bag semantics, or if a `DISTINCT` makes the difference invisible.
- **NULL.** The pure algebra has no NULL. SQL's three-valued logic means "the rows where p is true" plus "the rows where p is false" does not always give back the whole table: rows where p is *unknown* appear in neither.
- **Aggregation is an extension.** Grouping (written with the Greek letter γ, gamma) is not part of Codd's original algebra; textbooks add it as an extended operator.
- **No recursion.** A fixed finite expression in ordinary relational algebra cannot compute reachability for arbitrary graph size or unbounded depth. A known fixed depth can be expanded into a fixed number of joins; `WITH RECURSIVE` handles the unbounded case.

```formula
R ∪ R ≡ R
σ p (R) ∪ σ ¬p (R) ≡ R
γ year, COUNT(sid) (Student)
where
R: any relation
∪: union: relational tuples in either input, each listed once in pure algebra
≡: is equivalent to: always gives the same result. Both of the first two lines hold in pure algebra. In SQL the first fails under bag semantics (R UNION ALL R doubles the rows), and the second fails when p is unknown for some row because of a NULL
σ: selection: keep relational tuples where the condition is true
p: a condition, such as discount > 0.1
¬: not: ¬p is true exactly when p is false. In SQL, when p is unknown (because of a NULL), ¬p is unknown too
γ: grouping and aggregation (the Greek letter gamma): group by the attributes listed first, then compute the aggregates listed after them
year: the grouping attribute
COUNT: the aggregate that counts the values in each group
sid: the student-id attribute being counted
Student: the relation of students
In words: in pure algebra, a union with itself changes nothing and "p or not p" covers every relational tuple; the last line counts students per year, giving (1, 1), (2, 2) and (3, 1) for the running example.
```

## Key takeaways

- Bag multiplicities and NULL can invalidate pure-set identities.
- Aggregation extends the algebra; unbounded reachability needs recursion.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational model and algebra](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch2.pdf)
- [PostgreSQL 18: constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html)

questions.prompt:
`product` has 10 rows. `discount` is NULL in 2 of them. These queries return 3 rows and 5 rows:

```sql
SELECT * FROM product
WHERE discount > 0.1;

SELECT * FROM product
WHERE NOT (discount > 0.1);
```

Why do they not add up to 10?

options.text: The two queries overlap, so some rows are counted twice
options.explanation: A row cannot satisfy both p and NOT p. There is no overlap; rows are missing, not doubled.

options.text: `NOT` is applied after `WHERE`, so it filters the wrong rows
options.explanation: `NOT` is part of the predicate, evaluated per row inside `WHERE`.

options.text: For the 2 NULL rows the predicate is *unknown*, and `WHERE` keeps only rows where it is true, so the rows where p is true plus the rows where NOT p is true no longer make up the whole relation
options.explanation: Correct. Under SQL's three-valued logic, NOT unknown is still unknown. The NULL-discount rows appear in neither result. Classical algebra assumes two-valued logic, so this identity breaks.

options.text: The optimiser used different indexes, which return different rows
options.explanation: Different plans must return the same result; an index cannot change which rows satisfy a predicate.

questions.workedExample:
1. Non-NULL rows: 8. Of these, 3 have discount > 0.1 and 5 do not: 3 + 5 = 8.
2. NULL rows: `NULL > 0.1` is **unknown**; `NOT unknown` is **unknown**.
3. `WHERE` keeps only **true**, so the 2 NULL rows appear in neither query.
4. To cover everything: `WHERE NOT (discount > 0.1) OR discount IS NULL`, or `COALESCE(discount, 0) <= 0.1`.

lessons.title: What functional dependencies claim
lessons.summary: What functional dependencies claim, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
lessons.body:
Normalisation, covered in the later normal-form units, can sound like a list of rules to memorise. It is not. The normal forms 2NF, 3NF and BCNF are defined using **functional dependencies** (FDs); higher forms also involve multivalued or join dependencies. Once you can reason about FDs, normal forms become mechanical checks.

This unit establishes what an FD claims and how to refute a proposed one. The following units derive consequences, compute attribute closures and find every candidate key.

We use single capital letters for attribute names in abstract examples. Adjacent letters in a card denote an attribute set, never a numeric product; every card defines that convention locally.

## What a functional dependency says

A functional dependency is a universal rule comparing pairs of relational tuples, not a claim about one row in isolation:

> Any two relational tuples that agree on X must also agree on Y.

```formula
X → Y
for all t_1, t_2 in R:
  t_1[X] = t_2[X] gives t_1[Y] = t_2[Y]
where
X, Y: sets of attributes of R; each may be a single attribute or several
→: "functionally determines": the condition on the next two lines holds in every legal state of R
R: the relation (table) the dependency is about
t_1, t_2: any two relational tuples (rows) of R
t_1[X], t_2[X]: the values the relational tuple has for the attributes in X; t_1[Y] and t_2[Y] likewise for Y
In words: whenever two rows have the same X values, they must have the same Y values. Knowing X pins down Y.
```

Take a spreadsheet of enrolments that someone has imported as one table:

```
sid  sname  cid  ctitle      grade
 1   Ada    DB   Databases    A
 1   Ada    OS   Op Systems   B
 2   Ben    DB   Databases    C
```

The business rules say a student id identifies one name, a course code identifies one title, and there is one grade per student per course. As FDs:

```formula
sid → sname
cid → ctitle
{sid, cid} → grade
where
→: functionally determines: rows equal on the left side are equal on the right side
sid: the student id
sname: the student's name
cid: the course code
ctitle: the course title
grade: the grade the student got on that course
{ }: a set of attributes; {sid, cid} means "sid and cid together"
In words: the id fixes the name, the code fixes the title, and only the pair (student, course) fixes the grade.
```

An FD is a **constraint on every legal state**, exactly like a key. You get it from the domain, not from the data.

> [!warning] Data can refute an FD, never prove one
> If two rows share a `cid` but have different titles, the FD from `cid` to `ctitle` is false (or the data is dirty). But if today's rows all happen to have unique surnames, that does not make surname a determinant of anything. Data-profiling tools that "discover" FDs find candidates that a human must confirm.

### Trivial and non-trivial FDs

An FD is a **trivial FD** if its right side is part of its left side. Trivial FDs hold in every relation and tell you nothing. The interesting ones are non-trivial.

```formula
Y ⊆ X
{sid} ⊆ {sid, cid}
{sid, cid} → sid
where
X, Y: sets of attributes
→: functionally determines
⊆: "is a subset of": every attribute in Y is also in X (Y may equal X)
sid, cid: the student-id and course-code attributes
{ }: a set of attributes
In words: X → Y is called trivial exactly when Y ⊆ X. A set of attributes always determines any part of itself, so {sid, cid} → sid is true in every relation and says nothing.
```

### Keys are FDs too

A set K is a **superkey** of R exactly when K determines every attribute of R:

```formula
K → R
{sid, cid} → sname, ctitle, grade
where
K: a set of attributes of R
→: functionally determines
R: here, the set of all attributes of the relation R
sid, sname, cid, ctitle, grade: the attributes of the enrolment table above
{ }: a set of attributes
In words: K is a superkey when knowing K's values fixes every other value in the row.
```

Here the student id and course code together determine name, title and grade, so it is a superkey. Neither attribute alone determines everything, so it is also a **candidate key**: a superkey with nothing that can be removed.

The inference examples treat their stated FDs as the complete basis being analysed. Extra rules such as a singleton domain or a fixed maximum row count can imply additional dependencies; include those assumptions when deciding which states are legal.

## Key takeaways

- An FD constrains every pair of relational tuples in every legal state.
- Data can refute a proposed rule; a clean sample cannot establish it as a business constraint.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [PostgreSQL 18: constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html)


Trivial FDs come free from Armstrong's reflexivity rule.

lessons.title: Inferring dependencies with Armstrong rules
lessons.summary: Inferring dependencies with Armstrong rules, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
lessons.body:
## Armstrong's axioms

Given some FDs, which others must also hold? William Armstrong gave three inference rules in 1974. For attribute sets X, Y and Z:

1. **Reflexivity**: a set determines any subset of itself.
2. **Augmentation**: adding the same attributes to both sides keeps an FD true.
3. **Transitivity**: if X determines Y and Y determines Z, then X determines Z.

```formula
Y ⊆ X gives X → Y
X → Y gives XZ → YZ
X → Y and Y → Z gives X → Z
where
X, Y, Z: sets of attributes of one relation
⊆: is a subset of: every attribute of Y is in X
→: functionally determines
XZ, YZ: sets written side by side are combined: XZ means X ∪ Z, the attributes of X together with those of Z
∪: union: everything in either set
In words: line 1 is reflexivity, line 2 is augmentation and line 3 is transitivity.
```

The rules have **soundness** (every conclusion follows from the given FDs) and **completeness** (every FD that follows from those premises can be derived). Three useful rules follow from them: the **FD union rule**, the **decomposition rule** and **pseudotransitivity**.

```formula
X → Y and X → Z gives X → YZ
X → YZ gives X → Y and X → Z
X → Y and WY → Z gives WX → Z
where
W, X, Y, Z: sets of attributes of one relation
→: functionally determines
YZ, WY, WX: combined sets, for example YZ = Y ∪ Z
∪: union: everything in either set
In words: the FD union rule combines right sides that share a left side; decomposition splits a right side apart; pseudotransitivity chains two FDs when extra attributes W are needed on the second one's left.
```

> [!warning] The left side does not decompose
> A right side can be split, but a left side cannot. Grade depends on student *and* course together, not on either alone.

```formula
XY → Z ⇏ X → Z
{sid, cid} → grade ⇏ sid → grade
where
X, Y, Z: sets of attributes
XY: X ∪ Y, the two sets combined
∪: union
→: functionally determines
⇏: "does not imply": the left FD can hold while the right one fails
sid, cid, grade: the student-id, course-code and grade attributes
{ }: a set of attributes
In words: knowing that X and Y together determine Z tells you nothing about X alone. One student has several grades, one per course.
```

The **FD closure** contains every functional dependency implied by a given basis:

```formula
X → Y in F⁺ when F ⊨ X → Y
where
F: the set of FDs you were given
F⁺: the FD closure of F: every FD that follows logically from F, including the trivial ones
X, Y: sets of attributes
→: functionally determines
⊨: "logically implies": every relation state that satisfies all of F also satisfies X → Y
In words: F⁺ is everything you can derive from F with Armstrong's axioms.
```

F⁺ can be exponentially large, so in practice you never list it. You compute attribute closures instead.

## Key takeaways

- Reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity derive exactly the implied FDs.
- Right sides split; left sides generally do not. Counterexamples refute invalid inference.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [PostgreSQL 18: constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html)

lessons.title: Computing attribute closure
lessons.summary: Computing attribute closure, with complete worked examples and local definitions.
lessons.body:
## The attribute-closure algorithm

An **attribute closure** collects every attribute determined by a chosen starting set under the given FD basis. Compute it with a fixpoint loop:

1. Start with the requested attribute set as the result.
2. Find any FD in F whose whole left side is already inside result. Add its right side to result.
3. Repeat until nothing changes.

```formula
result_0 = X
M_k = ⋃{Y : (L → Y) in F, L ⊆ result_k}
result_{k+1} = result_k ∪ M_k
X⁺ = result_k when result_{k+1} = result_k
where
X: the attribute set whose attribute closure you want
X⁺: the attribute closure of X: every attribute X determines under F
F: the set of FDs
L, Y: left and right attribute sets of an FD in F
M_k: all right-side attributes whose left sides are already available at step k
⋃: union of every set in the collection, including the empty union when none qualifies
result_0, result_k, result_{k+1}: the set built so far: at the start, after k steps, and after one more step
k: the step number, 0, 1, 2, ...
∪: union: add all currently derivable right-side attributes
⊆: is a subset of: every attribute of L is already in the result
→: functionally determines
In words: keep firing any FD whose left side you already have, adding its right side, until no FD adds anything new. What you have then is X⁺.
```

The same algorithm in Python, with a set of letters standing for attributes:

```python
def closure(attrs, fds):
    # Start with the known attributes.
    result = set(attrs)
    changed = True
    while changed:
        changed = False
        # Fire every applicable dependency.
        for lhs, rhs in fds:
            if lhs <= result \
               and not rhs <= result:
                # Add new attributes.
                result |= rhs
                changed = True
    return result

F = [({'A'}, {'B'}),
     ({'B'}, {'C'}),
     ({'C', 'D'}, {'E'})]
print(sorted(closure({'A'}, F)))
# ['A', 'B', 'C']
print(sorted(closure({'A', 'D'}, F)))
# ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E']
```

Trace the attribute closure of {A, D} for R(A, B, C, D, E):

```formula
F = {A → B, B → C, CD → E}
{A, D}⁺ = {A, B, C, D, E}
where
R: a relation with five attributes, A, B, C, D and E
A, B, C, D, E: the attributes of R
F: the FDs that hold on R
CD: the set {C, D}
→: functionally determines
{ }: a set
{A, D}⁺: the attribute closure of {A, D}: everything A and D together determine
In words: starting from A and D, the three FDs fire in turn and reach every attribute.
```

The first dependency adds B to the known A and D. The second then adds C; with C and D available, the third adds E. A sequential Python pass can fire a later rule using an attribute added earlier in that same pass. The card uses simultaneous rounds instead: both schedules reach the same least fixed point.

Each pass of the loop either adds at least one attribute or changes nothing and stops, so the number of passes is bounded by the number of attributes:

```formula
N_pass ≤ |R| + 1
where
N_pass: the number of times the loop goes through all the FDs
|R|: the number of attributes of R (5 in the trace above)
≤: is at most
In words: at most one adding pass per attribute, plus a final pass that finds nothing to add. Each pass checks every FD once, so the whole algorithm runs in polynomial time and is fast in practice.
```

## Key takeaways

- Start from known attributes and apply every available FD until a full pass adds nothing.
- Sequential firing and simultaneous rounds reach the same least fixed point.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [PostgreSQL 18: constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html)

lessons.title: Applying attribute closure
lessons.summary: Applying attribute closure, with complete worked examples and local definitions.
lessons.body:
## Three jobs for attribute closure

1. **Does F imply a given FD?** Compute the attribute closure of its left side and check that the right side is inside it.
2. **Is X a superkey?** Yes exactly when its attribute closure is every attribute of R.
3. **Are F and G equivalent?** Yes if every FD in G follows from F, and every FD in F follows from G.

```formula
F ⊨ X → Y iff Y ⊆ X⁺
X⁺ = R
F ≡ G iff F⁺ = G⁺
{A, D}⁺ = ABCDE, so F ⊨ AD → E
A⁺ = {A, B, C}, so F ⊭ A → E
where
F, G: two sets of FDs over the same relation
X, Y: sets of attributes
→: functionally determines
⊨: logically implies; ⊭: does not imply
⊆: is a subset of
X⁺: the attribute closure of X under F
R: here, the set of all attributes of the relation (A, B, C, D, E in the example, with F = {A → B, B → C, CD → E})
≡: equivalent: F and G imply exactly the same FDs
F⁺, G⁺: the FD closures of F and G: every FD each one implies
A⁺, {A, D}⁺: the attribute closures of A and of {A, D} under F
A, B, C, D, E: the attributes of R
ABCDE, AD: the sets {A, B, C, D, E} and {A, D}
In words: line 1: F implies X → Y exactly when every attribute of Y is in the attribute closure of X ("iff" means "if and only if"). Line 2: X is a superkey exactly when its attribute closure is all of R. Line 3: F and G are equivalent exactly when they imply the same FDs. In the example, A and D together reach E, so AD → E follows from F; A alone only reaches A, B and C, so A → E does not.
```

In practice you test equivalence FD by FD: compute each FD's left-side attribute closure under the other set, rather than ever listing F⁺.

## Key takeaways

- The attribute closure of a determinant tests both implication and superkeys.
- Two FD sets are equivalent exactly when each derives all dependencies of the other.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [PostgreSQL 18: constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html)

1. Attributes never on a right side: A and B. They must be in every key.

```formula

  ∪ {D} by BC → D
  ∪ {E} by D → E
{A, B}⁺ = {A, B, C, D, E} = R

B⁺ = {B}
where

∪: union: add the attributes on the right

In words: A gives C; then B and C together give D; then D gives E. AB reaches everything, but A alone and B alone do not.
```
