lessons.title: Finding every candidate key
lessons.summary: Finding every candidate key, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
lessons.body:
## Finding candidate keys

A **candidate key** is a superkey with no unnecessary attributes:

```formula
X⁺ = R
X' ⊂ X gives X'⁺ ≠ R
where
X: the candidate key being tested
X⁺: the attribute closure of X
R: the set of all attributes of the relation
X': any set made by removing at least one attribute from X
⊂: is a proper subset of: contained in X but not equal to it
X'⁺: the attribute closure of X'
≠: is not equal to
In words: X determines everything, and no smaller part of X does.
```

Searching every subset is exponential, but two observations prune it hard:

- An attribute that **never appears on any right-hand side** cannot be derived, so it must be in **every** key.
- An attribute that appears **only on right-hand sides**, and in no determinant, is in **no** candidate key: starting with it cannot help derive anything else, so a superkey containing it can derive it from the other attributes. This assumes the stated FDs are the complete constraint basis being analysed.

> [!example] One key
> Use the five-attribute closure example from the preceding unit: A fixes B, B fixes C, and C together with D fixes E. A and D cannot be derived, so every key includes both. Their attribute closure reaches all five attributes; therefore that pair is the only candidate key. The exact FD basis and attribute closure are restated in the card below.

```formula
F = {A → B, B → C, CD → E}
{A, D}⁺ = {A, B, C, D, E}
where
F: the complete functional-dependency basis for this five-attribute example
A, B, C, D, E: the five attributes
CD: the set containing C and D
→: functionally determines
{A, D}⁺: attributes derivable from the pair A and D under F
{ }: a set of attributes
In words: A gives B and C, then C with D gives E. Neither A nor D can be derived, so every key must include both.
```

> [!example] Several keys
> In the four-attribute example below, B cannot be derived and therefore belongs to every key. B alone reaches only itself; adding any one of A, C or D reaches the whole heading.
>
> The candidate keys are B with A, B with C, and B with D. Each is a **prime attribute** (belongs to some candidate key), a fact the 3NF test in the next lesson cares about.

```formula
F = {AB → C, C → D, D → A}
B⁺ = {B}
{A, B}⁺ = {A, B, C, D}
{B, C}⁺ = {A, B, C, D}
{B, D}⁺ = {A, B, C, D}
where
A, B, C, D: the attributes of R
F: the FDs that hold on R
AB: the set {A, B}
→: functionally determines
B⁺, {A, B}⁺, {B, C}⁺, {B, D}⁺: attribute closures under F
{ }: a set
In words: AB uses AB → C then C → D; BC uses C → D then D → A; BD uses D → A then AB → C. Each reaches everything, and B alone does not, so all three are minimal.
```

A relation with n attributes can have exponentially many candidate keys. For schemas specified by an FD basis, Lucchesi and Osborn showed that deciding whether a given attribute is prime is NP-complete. Exhaustive enumeration can be practical for a small schema; larger ones may need pruning. This explains why identifying every prime attribute for the 3NF test can be harder than computing one attribute closure.

“Minimal” means minimal under set inclusion, not smallest cardinality among keys. There can be candidate keys of different sizes. When checking minimality of a superkey, it suffices to remove each member in turn: if any proper subset were a superkey, some single-member removal would also be one. Do not stop after finding the first candidate key; prime attributes depend on the union of all of them.

## Key takeaways

- Every key must include attributes that cannot be derived from right sides.
- Check every candidate for inclusion minimality; all candidate keys contribute prime attributes.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [PostgreSQL 18: constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html)

2. Only on a right side: E. So E is in no key.

```formula
D⁺ = {D, E}

→: functionally determines
{ }: a set
In words: D brings E; any one of A, B or C brings the other two round the cycle. So D plus any one of them reaches everything.
```

4. Each is minimal (D alone fails, and A, B, C alone cannot reach D).
5. Keys: **AD, BD, CD**.

lessons.title: Minimal FD covers and FD equivalence
lessons.summary: Minimal FD covers and FD equivalence, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
lessons.body:
## Minimal FD cover

Two FD sets can say the same thing with different amounts of redundancy. A **minimal FD cover** here means an equivalent set with singleton right sides and no remaining redundancy. Some texts call a grouped-right-side version a canonical FD cover; these presentation conventions differ, while the implied dependencies agree. Our singleton convention requires:

1. Every right side is a single attribute.
2. No left side has an **extraneous determinant attribute** (one you could drop and still derive the FD).
3. No FD is **redundant** (derivable from the others).

The card below starts with a dependency fixing two right-side attributes, a duplicate implied dependency, and an unnecessarily large determinant. Work through it in three stages:

1. Split the two-attribute right side into two dependencies; merge the duplicate dependency fixing B from A.
2. Test B in the two-attribute determinant. A alone already reaches C through B, so B adds nothing to that determinant. Reducing it produces another duplicate.
3. The remaining one-step functional dependency from A to C is implied by the two-step chain through B, so remove it.

```formula
F = {A → BC, B → C, A → B, AB → C}
F_1 = {A → B, A → C, B → C, AB → C}
A⁺ = {A, B, C}
F_2 = {A → B, A → C, B → C}
F_3 = {A → B, B → C}
where
A, B, C: attributes
F: the original set of FDs
BC, AB: the sets {B, C} and {A, B}
→: functionally determines
F_1: F after splitting every right side into single attributes
A⁺: the attribute closure of A; it contains C, so B is extraneous in AB → C
F_2: F_1 with AB → C reduced to A → C (now a duplicate, so merged)
F_3: F_2 without A → C, which follows from A → B and B → C by transitivity
{ }: a set
In words: four FDs reduce to two with exactly the same meaning: F_3 is a minimal FD cover of F.
```

The two dependencies in the final card line form a minimal FD cover. Four FDs became two, with exactly the same meaning. The 3NF synthesis algorithm in the next lesson starts from a minimal FD cover, which is why this step matters. Minimal FD covers are not always unique; different removal orders can give different, equally valid answers.

## Key takeaways

- A singleton-right-side minimal FD cover removes extraneous left attributes and redundant dependencies.
- Equivalent covers have the same implications and need not be unique.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [PostgreSQL 18: constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html)

```formula
BC, AB: the sets {B, C} and {A, B}
→: functionally determines: rows that agree on the left side agree on the right side
{ }: a set
In words: A fixes B and C; B fixes C; A and B together fix D. A minimal FD cover is an equivalent set with single-attribute right sides, no unneeded left attributes and no redundant FDs.
```

questions.workedExample:
Split right sides, remove B from the determinant fixing D, and then remove the direct A-to-C dependency implied through B. The resulting set is equivalent in both directions:

```formula
A⁺ = {A, B, C, D}
F_1 = {A → B, A → C, B → C, A → D}
F_2 = {A → B, B → C, A → D}
A⁺ with F_2 = {A, B, C, D}
where
A⁺: the attribute closure of A: everything A determines
A, B, C, D: attributes
→: functionally determines
F_1: F with right sides split and AB → D reduced to A → D (B was extraneous, since A⁺ already contains D)

In words: dropping B from AB → D and dropping A → C changes nothing: A still reaches everything. Removing A → B would leave A⁺ = {A, D}, so A → B is needed; B → C and A → D are needed too.
```

The final card line is the minimal FD cover; no remaining dependency or left attribute can be removed.

lessons.title: Dependencies in PostgreSQL queries
lessons.summary: Dependencies in PostgreSQL queries, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
lessons.body:
## Where FDs show up in real systems

- **Keys and UNIQUE constraints** directly enforce key-based dependencies. SQL has no general FUNCTIONAL DEPENDENCY declaration for an arbitrary dependency between two sets of columns; some special dependencies can be enforced with CHECK or exclusion constraints, and others need triggers or schema decomposition. Normalisation avoids storing the same dependent fact in many rows.
- **Postgres uses FDs in GROUP BY.** If you group by a table's primary key, PostgreSQL 16–18 lets you select that table's other columns without listing them, because it knows the key determines them:

```sql
SELECT c.id, c.name, COUNT(*)
FROM customer c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
-- Grouping the PK fixes the name.
GROUP BY c.id;
```

- **Optimisers use FDs** to drop redundant grouping or sorting columns and to prove that a join cannot multiply rows.
- **Data-quality checks** test candidate FDs against stored rows. With both `cid` and `ctitle` constrained `NOT NULL`, grouping by course code and requiring more than one distinct title finds violations. `COUNT(DISTINCT ...)` ignores NULLs; do not silently treat its result as an FD proof when missing titles are allowed.

```sql
-- Find codes with conflicting titles.
SELECT cid FROM sheet
GROUP BY cid
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT ctitle) > 1;
```

## Common mistakes

- **Reading FDs off sample data.** A coincidence in 50 rows is not a rule.
- **Splitting the left side.** Two attributes determining a third together does not imply that either one does alone.
- **Forgetting transitivity.** When asked for keys, compute the attribute closure; do not eyeball it. Chains through two FDs are easy to miss.
- **Stopping at one key.** A relation can have several candidate keys, and normal-form tests depend on all of them.

```formula
XY → Z ⇏ X → Z
D → A and AB → C gives BD → C
where
X, Y, Z: sets of attributes
XY: X ∪ Y, the two sets combined
∪: union
→: functionally determines
⇏: does not imply
A, B, C, D: single attributes
AB, BD: the sets {A, B} and {B, D}
In words: the first line is the left-side mistake; the second is an easily missed chain: D gives A, and then A with B gives C.
```

## Key takeaways

- PostgreSQL recognises its base-table primary-key grouping rule, not every logically inferable FD.
- Distinct-value checks can refute an FD when missing values are handled explicitly.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [PostgreSQL 18: constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html)

questions.prompt:
In Postgres, `customer(id PRIMARY KEY, name)` and `orders(id, customer_id)`. Which query fails with "column must appear in the GROUP BY clause"?

```sql
-- Q1
SELECT c.id, c.name, COUNT(*)
FROM customer c JOIN orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id;

-- Q2
SELECT o.customer_id, c.name,
       COUNT(*)
FROM customer c JOIN orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY o.customer_id;
```

options.text: Q1 only
options.explanation: Q1 groups by customer's primary key, so Postgres knows c.name is functionally dependent on it and allows it.

options.text: Q2 only
options.explanation: Correct. Postgres only recognises the FD from a table's primary key to the other columns of the same table. o.customer_id equals c.id in every row, but Postgres does not reason through the join condition, so c.name is rejected.

options.text: Both
options.explanation: Q1 is accepted thanks to Postgres's functional-dependency rule for primary keys.

options.text: Neither
options.explanation: Q2 is rejected; Postgres does not infer FDs through join equalities.

questions.workedExample:
1. PostgreSQL 16–18 rule for these base tables: an ungrouped column is allowed if the grouped columns include the **primary key of that column's table**.
2. Q1: groups by c.id, the PK of customer, so c.name is allowed.
3. Q2: groups by o.customer_id. It is equal to c.id in every joined row, so logically c.name is determined, but Postgres does not use that inference.
4. Fix Q2: keep o.customer_id grouped and add c.id, or add c.name: `GROUP BY o.customer_id, c.id` / `GROUP BY o.customer_id, c.name`.

options.text: `SELECT cid FROM sheet GROUP BY cid HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`
options.explanation: This finds codes that appear more than once, which is normal: many students take the same course. Repetition is not a violation; disagreement is.

options.text: `SELECT cid FROM sheet GROUP BY cid HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT ctitle) > 1`
options.explanation: Correct. It finds codes associated with more than one distinct title, which is exactly two relational tuples equal on cid but different on ctitle.

options.text: `SELECT DISTINCT cid, ctitle FROM sheet`
options.explanation: This lists the pairs, but you would still have to inspect them by eye to find codes appearing with two titles.

options.text: `SELECT ctitle FROM sheet GROUP BY ctitle HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT cid) > 1`
options.explanation: That tests whether a title fixes the course code, reversing the required direction. Two course codes sharing a title do not violate the original rule.

questions.workedExample:
1. A violation has equal course codes associated with different titles.
2. Group by X (`cid`) and count distinct Y (`ctitle`).
3. Any group with `COUNT(DISTINCT ctitle) > 1` is a violation.
4. Note: `COUNT(DISTINCT ...)` ignores NULLs, so a code with one title and some NULL titles will not show up. Add `OR COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE ctitle IS NULL) > 0` if NULLs matter.

lessons.title: Anomalies and first normal form
lessons.summary: Anomalies and first normal form, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
lessons.body:
Normalisation is the process of splitting a badly structured relation into smaller ones so that **each fact is stored once**. When a fact is stored in many rows, the copies can disagree unless additional constraints or coordinated writes keep them consistent.

Each normal form forbids one kind of redundancy, defined precisely with the functional dependencies (FDs) from the previous lesson. Kent’s informal summary says that non-key facts should depend on the key, its whole value, and no unrelated determinant. It is a mnemonic; the precise prime-attribute conditions in the following units handle cases the mnemonic misses.

The formula below states the business rules. Every card defines its notation locally; an arrow expresses a rule across all legal states, rather than a coincidence in these three rows.

## The problem: anomalies

A shop imports its order spreadsheet as a single table:

```
OrderLine
oid pid odate  cid cname pname  price qty
 10 P1  03-01  C7  Ann   Bolt   0.20  50
 10 P2  03-01  C7  Ann   Nut    0.10  50
 11 P1  03-02  C9  Raj   Bolt   0.20  10
```

The business rules, as FDs:

```formula
oid → odate, cid
cid → cname
pid → pname, price
{oid, pid} → qty
where
→: functionally determines: rows that agree on the left side must agree on the right side
oid: the order id
odate: the order date
cid: the customer id
cname: the customer's name
pid: the product id
pname: the product's name
price: the product's current price (this shop sets one current price per product)
qty: the quantity of that product on that order
, (on the right of →): both attributes are determined, so oid → odate, cid means oid → {odate, cid}
{ }: a set of attributes; {oid, pid} means "order and product together"
In words: an order has one date and one customer; a customer has one name; a product has one name and price; and the quantity belongs to an order and product together.
```

The only candidate key is the pair of order id and product id. Three kinds of trouble follow.

1. **Update anomaly.** Ann changes her name. It is stored on every line of every order she has placed, and an update that misses one leaves the data contradicting itself.
2. **Insertion anomaly.** You cannot record a new product until someone orders it, because `oid` is part of the key and cannot be NULL.
3. **Deletion anomaly.** Delete order 11, Raj's only order, and you lose the fact that customer C9 is called Raj.

All three come from FDs whose left side is not a key: the table is storing facts about customers and products inside rows about order lines.

## First normal form (1NF)

A relation is in 1NF when every attribute value is an **atomic relational value**: a single value from its domain, with no repeating groups.

```
Not 1NF
oid  products
 10  "P1:50, P2:50"
```

Ordinary column constraints and joins do not directly represent the individual items; string-splitting expressions or custom constraints are more complex than storing a row per item. The fix is one row per product per order, as in OrderLine above.

> [!note] What counts as atomic?
> Atomicity is relative to the chosen domains and relational presentation. Decomposability by a function does not alone violate 1NF: dates and text have inspectable parts. Under the classical flat-relation convention used here, a repeating collection of phone numbers or order lines is represented by separate relational tuples. SQL arrays and JSON are valid SQL values with useful operators, but calling them automatically in or out of 1NF merely because an application searches inside them is too broad. For this design, separate rows let each phone or line have ordinary keys, foreign keys and indexes.

## Key takeaways

- Mixing order, customer and product facts creates update, insertion and deletion anomalies.
- Use separate relational tuples for repeating phone or item facts under the flat relational convention.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [Fagin: multivalued dependencies and fourth normal form](https://research.ibm.com/publications/multivalued-dependencies-and-a-new-normal-form-for-relational-databases)

questions.prompt: A single flat `OrderLine` table repeats customer id `cid` and name `cname` on each order/product line. Its key is the order id `oid` together with product id `pid`. Customer C9 (Raj) appears only on order 11. You delete order 11, which is Raj's only order. Afterwards nobody can find out what customer C9 is called. Which anomaly is this?

options.text: Update anomaly
options.explanation: An update anomaly is about changing one fact that is stored in many rows and missing a copy. Nothing was updated here.

options.text: Insertion anomaly
options.explanation: An insertion anomaly is being unable to record a fact (for example a new customer) without an unrelated one (an order).

options.text: Deletion anomaly
options.explanation: Correct. Deleting one fact (the order) unintentionally deleted another (the customer's name), because both lived in the same rows.

options.text: Referential integrity violation
options.explanation: No foreign key is broken; there is no separate Customer table to reference yet. That is exactly the design problem.

questions.workedExample:
1. `cname` depends on non-key cid; the key {oid, pid} also determines it transitively.
2. So customer facts exist only as a side effect of order lines.
3. Remove Raj's last line and the fact "C9 is Raj" goes with it: a **deletion anomaly**.
4. After normalising, `Customer(cid, cname)` keeps Raj even with no orders.

questions.prompt: A `contact` table has a column `phones` holding values like `'020 7946 0000; 07700 900123'`. Support staff need to search for a customer by any one phone number. Under the classical flat-relation convention, where each phone is a separate domain value rather than a collection, which normal form is being violated, and what is the usual fix?

options.text: 2NF; move phones into a table keyed by part of the primary key
options.explanation: 2NF is about partial dependencies on a composite key. The problem here is a non-atomic relational value inside one column.

options.text: 1NF; store one row per phone number in a `contact_phone(contact_id, phone)` table
options.explanation: Correct. The column holds a repeating group. Because staff must search on a single number, each number should be its own value, which also lets you index and constrain it.

options.text: 3NF; phones depend transitively on the contact's id
options.explanation: There is no transitive dependency here. The issue is that one attribute value holds several values.

options.text: None; a semicolon-separated string is atomic because it is one text value
options.explanation: A SQL text value can contain delimiters, and searching inside text does not by itself define 1NF. Under the classical flat representation stipulated here, however, the phone-number collection is a repeating group; separate rows provide ordinary indexing and per-number constraints.

questions.workedExample:
1. 1NF requires atomic relational values, with no repeating groups.
2. The modelling requirement is one searchable, constrainable phone-number fact per row. Querying a component of a value does not universally determine atomicity: dates and text have components too. Separate phone rows implement the flat convention and the stated requirement.
3. Fix:

```sql
CREATE TABLE contact_phone (
  contact_id INT REFERENCES contact,
  phone      TEXT,
  PRIMARY KEY (contact_id, phone));
```

4. For efficient searches by phone alone, add an index on phone. The composite primary-key index starts with contact_id; a planner may scan it or use skip scan, but a direct phone index is the straightforward access path.

lessons.title: Second normal form and partial dependence
lessons.summary: Second normal form and partial dependence, with complete worked examples and local definitions.
lessons.body:
This unit continues the shop design: an order line stores order id `oid`, product id `pid`, date `odate`, customer id `cid`, customer name `cname`, product name `pname`, current product price `price`, and quantity `qty`. An order has one customer and date; a product has one current name and price. One line per order and product is the business rule.

## Second normal form (2NF)

A relation is in 2NF when it is in 1NF and **no non-prime attribute depends on part of a candidate key**. (A **prime** attribute is one that belongs to some candidate key.)

```formula
X ↛ A
  for every X ⊂ K and every A ∉ P
where
K: any candidate key of the relation
X: a set of attributes that is part of K but not all of it
⊂: is a proper subset of: inside K, and smaller than K
A: a single attribute
P: the set of prime attributes: those that belong to at least one candidate key
∉: is not a member of; A ∉ P means A is non-prime
↛: does not functionally determine
In words: no non-prime attribute may be determined by only part of a candidate key.
```

In the usual case with no constant non-prime attributes, a single-attribute candidate key has no non-empty proper part, so partial dependence needs a composite key. Formally the empty attribute set is also a proper subset; a non-prime attribute forced constant can therefore violate the fully general predicate even with a singleton key. The worked schemas have no such constant dependencies. OrderLine’s key is the order/product pair, and each half determines attributes on its own:

```formula
oid → odate, cid, cname
pid → pname, price
where
→: functionally determines
oid, pid: the order id and product id, each one half of the key {oid, pid}
odate, cid, cname: the order date, customer id and customer name (oid reaches cname through cid)
pname, price: the product's name and current price
In words: the order id alone fixes the date and customer; the product id alone fixes the product's name and price.
```

Both are **partial dependencies**. Fix them by moving each one into its own relation:

```formula
Order(oid, odate, cid, cname)
Product(pid, pname, price)
Line(oid, pid, qty)
where
Order: the relation of orders, with the attributes shown
Customer: the relation of customers
Product: the relation of products
Line: the relation of order lines
OrderLine: the original combined order-line relation
oid: order identifier
odate: order date
cid: customer identifier
cname: customer name
pid: product identifier
pname: product name
price: current product price, in pounds per item
qty: number of items ordered
In words: these are the headings after moving dependent customer and product facts into their own relations.
```

## Key takeaways

- 2NF forbids a non-prime attribute depending on a proper part of any candidate key.
- Separate order and product facts from order-line facts to remove partial dependencies.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [Fagin: multivalued dependencies and fourth normal form](https://research.ibm.com/publications/multivalued-dependencies-and-a-new-normal-form-for-relational-databases)

questions.prompt:
A relation with attributes A, B, C is in 1NF and has only the following non-trivial dependency as its complete FD basis. Its only candidate key is the pair A and B. Which is the highest normal form R satisfies?

```formula
A → C
where
A, C: attributes of R
→: functionally determines: rows that agree on A must agree on C
In words: A alone fixes C, even though the key is A and B together.
```

options.text: 1NF
options.explanation: Correct. C is non-prime and depends on A, which is only part of the key {A, B}. That partial dependency breaks 2NF.

options.text: 2NF
options.explanation: 2NF forbids exactly this: a non-prime attribute (C) depending on part of a candidate key (A).

options.text: 3NF
options.explanation: 3NF implies 2NF, and 2NF already fails.

options.text: BCNF
options.explanation: A alone is not a superkey, so its non-trivial dependency fixing C also violates BCNF.

questions.workedExample:
1. Key: {A, B}. Prime attributes: A, B. Non-prime: C.
2. The stated dependency has determinant A, a proper part of the key, right side C is non-prime. That is a partial dependency.
3. So 2NF fails, and therefore 3NF and BCNF fail too.
4. R is only in **1NF**. Fix: split into (A, C) and (A, B).

lessons.title: Third normal form and indirect facts
lessons.summary: Third normal form and indirect facts, with complete worked examples and local definitions.
lessons.body:
The shop has already separated order lines from product facts. Its remaining Order relation stores order identifier `oid`, order date `odate`, customer identifier `cid` and customer name `cname`. An order fixes its date and customer; a customer fixes one current name. The only candidate key of Order is its order identifier.

## Third normal form (3NF)

A relation is in 3NF when, for every non-trivial FD whose right side is a single attribute A, **either the left side X is a superkey or A is prime**:

```formula
for every X → A in F⁺ with A ∉ X:
  X⁺ = R  or  A ∈ P
where
F⁺: every FD that holds on the relation (all FDs implied by the given set F)
X: the left side, a set of attributes
A: the right side, a single attribute
→: functionally determines
∉: is not a member of; A ∉ X makes the FD non-trivial
X⁺: the attribute closure of X; X⁺ = R means X is a superkey
R: the set of all attributes of the relation
∈: is a member of
P: the set of prime attributes (those in some candidate key)
In words: every real dependency either comes from a superkey or points at a key attribute.
```

The Order relation containing order id, date, customer id and customer name is in 2NF under these rules (its only candidate key is the single order id) but still repeats Ann's name on every order. The cause is a **transitive dependency**:

```formula
oid → cid and cid → cname
cid⁺ = {cid, cname}
where
→: functionally determines
oid: the order id, the key of Order
cid: the customer id
cname: the customer's name
cid⁺: the attribute closure of cid within Order
{ }: a set of attributes
In words: the order fixes the customer, and the customer fixes the name, so the name hangs off the key only indirectly. cid reaches just cid and cname, not all of Order, so it is not a superkey.
```

`cid` is not a superkey of Order and `cname` is not prime, so 3NF is violated. Split again:

```formula
Order(oid, odate, cid)
Customer(cid, cname)
Product(pid, pname, price)
Line(oid, pid, qty)
where
Order: the relation of orders, with the attributes shown
Customer: the relation of customers
Product: the relation of products
Line: the relation of order lines
OrderLine: the original combined order-line relation
oid: order identifier
odate: order date
cid: customer identifier
cname: customer name
pid: product identifier
pname: product name
price: current product price, in pounds per item
qty: number of items ordered
In words: these are the headings after moving dependent customer and product facts into their own relations.
```

Now every FD's left side is a key of its relation. Ann's name lives in one row, products can exist before anyone orders them, and deleting an order loses nothing else.

> [!warning] Price is a different fact
> The current price of a product (one per product) can hold in every database state even when prices change over time. It does not imply that the price *paid* on every historical order line equals today's price. In a real shop, the price charged on an order is a separate fact from the current list price, and it belongs to the order and product together: the order id and product id together determine `price_paid`. Store it on `Line`. That is not denormalisation; it is modelling a time-dependent fact correctly. Normalising away the price paid is a classic bug that silently alters old invoices.

## Key takeaways

- 3NF checks every non-trivial singleton-right-side FD for a superkey determinant or prime result attribute.
- Customer name and historical price paid belong to different facts and require different determinants.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [Fagin: multivalued dependencies and fourth normal form](https://research.ibm.com/publications/multivalued-dependencies-and-a-new-normal-form-for-relational-databases)

questions.prompt:
A relation with attributes A, B, C, D is in 1NF and has these functional dependencies as its complete FD basis. What is the highest normal form R satisfies?

```formula
F = {A → B, B → C, A → D}
where
F: the set of functional dependencies on R
A, B, C, D: the attributes of R
→: functionally determines: rows that agree on the left side agree on the right side
{ }: a set
In words: A fixes B and D, and B fixes C.
```

options.text: 1NF
options.explanation: The key is the single attribute A, so no attribute can depend on *part* of a key. 2NF holds automatically.

options.text: 2NF
options.explanation: Correct. A is the only key, and no constant dependency is present, so 2NF holds. B fixes C while being neither a superkey nor determining a prime right-side attribute, so 3NF fails.

options.text: 3NF
options.explanation: The dependency fixing C from B violates 3NF: B is not a superkey and C is non-prime.

options.text: BCNF
options.explanation: The non-trivial dependency fixing C from B has a determinant that is not a superkey, so BCNF fails.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
A⁺ = {A, B, C, D}
B⁺ = {B, C}
where
A⁺, B⁺: the attribute closures of A and B: everything each determines under F = {A → B, B → C, A → D}
A, B, C, D: the attributes of R
→: functionally determines
{ }: a set
In words: A reaches every attribute, so it is a key; B reaches only itself and C, so it is not a superkey.
```

1. Keys: A is never on a right side and its attribute closure is everything, so **A is the only key**. Prime: A.
2. 2NF: with a one-attribute key there are no partial dependencies. Holds.
3. 3NF: check the dependency fixing C from B. Is B a superkey? No. Is C prime? No. **Violation.** (The key reaches C indirectly through B.)
4. Highest NF: **2NF**. Fix by splitting into (B, C) and (A, B, D).

lessons.title: BCNF and prime attributes
lessons.summary: BCNF and prime attributes, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
lessons.body:
## Boyce–Codd normal form (BCNF)

A relation is in BCNF when, for every non-trivial FD that holds in it, **the left side is a superkey**. BCNF drops 3NF's escape clause "or A is prime":

```formula
for every X → Y in F⁺ with Y ⊄ X:
  X⁺ = R
where
F⁺: every FD that holds on the relation
X, Y: sets of attributes, the left and right sides
→: functionally determines
⊄: is not a subset of; Y ⊄ X makes the FD non-trivial
X⁺: the attribute closure of X
R: the set of all attributes of the relation
In words: every real dependency must come from a superkey, with no exceptions.
```

3NF and BCNF differ only when a relation has overlapping candidate keys. The classic example: each teacher teaches one course, and each student has one teacher per course. Teaching records student, course and teacher:

```formula
{student, course} → teacher
teacher → course
K_1 = {student, course}
K_2 = {student, teacher}
teacher⁺ = {teacher, course}
where
student, course, teacher: the three attributes of Teaching
→: functionally determines
{ }: a set of attributes
K_1, K_2: the two candidate keys; they overlap on student
teacher⁺: the attribute closure of teacher
In words: a student and course fix the teacher, and a teacher fixes the course. teacher reaches only itself and course, so it is not a superkey.
```

- The FD from `teacher` to `course` has a left side that is not a superkey, so **BCNF fails**.
- But `course` is prime (it is in the first candidate key), so **3NF holds**.

The redundancy is real: "Smith teaches DB" is repeated for every student Smith teaches.

## Key takeaways

- BCNF requires a superkey determinant for every non-trivial FD.
- Teaching passes 3NF through a prime course attribute while still failing BCNF.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [Fagin: multivalued dependencies and fourth normal form](https://research.ibm.com/publications/multivalued-dependencies-and-a-new-normal-form-for-relational-databases)

questions.prompt:
`Teaching(student, course, teacher)` has these functional dependencies. Which statement is correct?

```formula
{student, course} → teacher
teacher → course
where
student, course, teacher: the attributes of Teaching
→: functionally determines: rows that agree on the left side agree on the right side
{ }: a set of attributes: student and course together
In words: a student has one teacher per course, and each teacher teaches one course.
```

options.text: It is not in 3NF, because the teacher-to-course dependency is transitive
options.explanation: 3NF permits a dependency with a non-superkey determinant when its right-hand attribute is prime. Course belongs to the student/course candidate key.

options.text: It is in BCNF, because every attribute is prime
options.explanation: BCNF does not care whether attributes are prime: it requires every non-trivial FD's left side to be a superkey, and teacher is not.

options.text: It is not even in 2NF
options.explanation: 2NF only restricts non-prime attributes, and all three attributes here are prime.

options.text: It is in 3NF but not BCNF
options.explanation: Correct. Both the student/course pair and the student/teacher pair are candidate keys. Teacher alone fixes course but not student: this fails BCNF while passing 3NF because course is prime.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
{student, course}⁺
  = {student, course, teacher}
{student, teacher}⁺
  = {student, course, teacher}
teacher⁺ = {teacher, course}
where
{student, course}⁺, {student, teacher}⁺, teacher⁺: attribute closures under the two FDs ({student, course} → teacher and teacher → course)
student, course, teacher: the attributes of Teaching
→: functionally determines
{ }: a set of attributes
In words: both pairs reach every attribute, so both are keys (student is never on a right side, so it must be in every key). teacher alone reaches only course, so it is not a superkey.
```

1. Keys: {student, course} and {student, teacher}, both minimal.
2. Prime attributes: student, course, teacher (all three).
3. BCNF test on the teacher-to-course dependency: teacher is not a superkey. **Fails.**
4. 3NF test: left side not a superkey, but course is prime. **Passes.**
5. So 3NF, not BCNF. The redundancy: "Smith teaches DB" repeats for each of Smith's students.

lessons.title: Lossless joins and dependency preservation
lessons.summary: Lossless joins and dependency preservation, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
lessons.body:
## Decomposing safely

Splitting a relation has two possible costs, and you should check both.

### Lossless join

A decomposition of R into R1 and R2 has a **lossless join** if joining the parts always gives back exactly R. If not, the join invents **spurious tuples**. The test for two parts:

```formula
r = π R_1 (r) ⋈ π R_2 (r)
  for every r in L
iff (R_1 ∩ R_2) → R_1 in F⁺
  or (R_1 ∩ R_2) → R_2 in F⁺
where
r: an instance of the original relation
L: all finite instances on the original heading satisfying the given functional dependencies
R_1, R_2: attribute sets covering the original heading
F: the given functional dependencies; this exact binary criterion assumes constraints consist of FDs
π: projection onto the following attribute set
⋈: natural join: match relational tuples on the shared attributes
∩: intersection: the attributes the two parts share
→: functionally determines
F⁺: every FD that holds on R
In words: the split has a lossless join when the shared attributes are a superkey of at least one side.
```

Split Teaching badly into `(student, course)` and `(course, teacher)`:

```
student course | course teacher
Ann     DB     | DB     Smith
Bob     DB     | DB     Jones
```

Joining on `course` produces four rows, including `Ann, DB, Jones`, which never happened. Then try the split into `(teacher, course)` and `(student, teacher)`:

```formula
R_1 ∩ R_2 = {course}
course⁺ = {course}
R_3 ∩ R_4 = {teacher}
teacher⁺ = {teacher, course}
where
R_1, R_2: the bad split, (student, course) and (course, teacher)
R_3, R_4: the good split, (teacher, course) and (student, teacher)
student, course, teacher: the attributes of Teaching
∩: intersection: the shared attributes
{ }: a set of attributes
course⁺, teacher⁺: attribute closures under {student, course} → teacher and teacher → course
→: functionally determines
In words: in the bad split the shared attribute course determines neither side, so the split is lossy. In the good split teacher determines course, which covers the whole of (teacher, course), so it gives a lossless join.
```

### Dependency preservation

A decomposition **preserves dependencies** if the FDs that hold inside each part, taken together, imply every FD in F:

```formula
(F_1 ∪ F_2 ∪ ... ∪ F_n)⁺ = F⁺
where
F: the original FDs
F⁺: every FD implied by F
n: the number of parts
F_1, F_2, F_n: the FDs from F⁺ that mention only attributes of part 1, part 2, ..., part n
...: and so on, for every part in between
∪: union: all the FDs together
In words: everything F says can still be checked one table at a time, without joining.
```

Enforcing those local dependencies then suffices without checking a join; an original FD can follow transitively across several local dependencies rather than literally fit in one part. The lossless-join BCNF split of Teaching loses the rule that a student and course together fix the teacher: the projected local FDs do not imply that original rule. For example, local keys still allow Ann to reference Smith and Jones while both teach DB. Merely observing that no part contains all three attributes is not a proof of non-preservation: some dependencies can follow transitively across parts.

## Key takeaways

- Losslessness concerns reconstructing every legal relation without invented relational tuples.
- Dependency preservation concerns whether projected local FDs together imply the original rules.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [Fagin: multivalued dependencies and fourth normal form](https://research.ibm.com/publications/multivalued-dependencies-and-a-new-normal-form-for-relational-databases)

```formula
F: the set of functional dependencies on R
A, B: attributes of R (C is the third)
→: functionally determines: rows that agree on A must agree on B
{ }: a set
In words: A fixes B; nothing else is known. In the options, A⁺ is the attribute closure of A and ⊇ means "contains".
```

```formula
R_1 ∩ R_2 → R_1 in F⁺
  or R_1 ∩ R_2 → R_2 in F⁺
A⁺ = {A, B} ⊇ R_1 = {A, B}
```

lessons.title: BCNF decomposition and 3NF synthesis
lessons.summary: BCNF decomposition and 3NF synthesis, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
lessons.body:
## The BCNF decomposition algorithm

1. Find a non-trivial dependency whose determinant is not a superkey of the current schema. The card calls that determinant X and the current heading S. Replace the current schema with the two parts shown.
2. Repeat until every relation is in BCNF.

```formula
S_1 = X⁺ ∩ S
S_2 = X ∪ (S − X⁺)
S_1 ∩ S_2 = X
where
S: the relation being split, as a set of attributes
X: the left side of an FD that violates BCNF in S
X⁺: the attribute closure of X under the dependencies projected onto the current schema S; equivalently compute the original attribute closure then intersect with S
∩: intersection: attributes in both
∪: union: attributes in either
−: difference: attributes of S that X does not determine
S_1: X plus everything in S that X determines
S_2: X plus everything else in S
In words: put X with what it determines in one part, and X with the rest in the other.
```

Each split shares exactly X, and X determines the whole first part, so every step gives a lossless join. In the five-attribute example below, A fixes B, B fixes C, and C together with D fixes E. Its only candidate key is the pair A and D:

```formula
A⁺ = {A, B, C}
A⁺ ∩ ABCDE = ABC
A ∪ (ABCDE − A⁺) = ADE
B⁺ ∩ ABC = BC
B ∪ (ABC − B⁺) = AB
where
A, B, C, D, E: the attributes of R; R itself is the set ABCDE
ABCDE, ABC, ADE, BC, AB: sets of attributes written as letters side by side, e.g. ABC = {A, B, C}
A⁺, B⁺: attribute closures under F = {A → B, B → C, CD → E}; B⁺ = {B, C}
{ }: a set
∩, ∪, −: intersection, union and difference of attribute sets
In words: A → B breaks BCNF (A is not a key), so ABCDE splits into ABC and ADE. Inside ABC, B → C breaks it (B is not a key), so ABC splits into BC and AB. ADE only has AD → E, and AD is its key.
```

The same split sequence as a schema sketch, with names grouping attributes:

```diagram
Full heading
  |  split on A
  +-- A B C
  |     |  split on B
  |     +-- B C
  |     +-- A B
  +-- A D E
```


All three are in BCNF and the decomposition is lossless-join, but the original rule that C and D together fix E is lost. The combined projected FDs cannot derive it: starting from C and D adds nothing in the local dependency union, so E is not reached.

## The 3NF synthesis algorithm

3NF can always be reached **losslessly while preserving every FD**. The synthesis algorithm (Bernstein, 1976):

1. Compute a minimal FD cover of F.
2. Make one relation for each left side X, containing X and everything it determines in the cover.
3. If no relation contains a candidate key of R, add one that is just a key.
4. Drop any relation that is a subset of another.

The original three dependencies are already a singleton-right-side minimal FD cover. Use that cover for the same five-attribute example:

```formula
A → B gives R_1 = AB
B → C gives R_2 = BC
CD → E gives R_3 = CDE
{A, D}⁺ = ABCDE gives R_4 = AD
where
A, B, C, D, E: the attributes of R
→: functionally determines
CD: the set {C, D}
R_1, R_2, R_3: one relation per FD of the minimal FD cover
AB, BC, CDE, AD, ABCDE: sets of attributes, letters side by side
{A, D}⁺: the attribute closure of {A, D}; it is everything, so AD is a candidate key
R_4: the extra relation holding just the key, added because AD is in none of R_1 to R_3
In words: one table per dependency, plus a table holding a key to tie them together.
```

Result: AB, BC, CDE, AD. Every FD lives in one relation, the key relation AD makes the decomposition lossless-join, and here each part happens to be in BCNF too.

## Choosing between 3NF and BCNF

| | 3NF | BCNF |
|---|---|---|
| Lossless join | always | always |
| FDs preserved | always | not always |
| Redundancy | a little possible | none from FDs |

Check the actual dependencies rather than assuming a frequency of overlapping keys. Many ordinary schemas can reach BCNF while preserving the required FDs; when those goals clash, the choices are:

- Stay in 3NF and accept some redundancy, enforcing the dependencies locally; keys alone may not express every local FD.
- Go to BCNF and enforce the lost FD another way, such as a trigger, a carefully synchronised trigger or application protocol that checks the joined rule. PostgreSQL ordinary views do not provide general declarative cross-table assertions; a naive check-then-write can race with another transaction.

## Key takeaways

- BCNF decomposition preserves lossless reconstruction but can lose dependencies.
- 3NF synthesis uses a minimal FD cover and adds a candidate-key relation when needed.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [Fagin: multivalued dependencies and fourth normal form](https://research.ibm.com/publications/multivalued-dependencies-and-a-new-normal-form-for-relational-databases)

questions.prompt:
Apply the BCNF decomposition algorithm to a relation with attributes A, B, C, D with the dependencies below. What is the result, and does it preserve all FDs?

```formula
F = {AB → C, C → D}
where
F: the set of functional dependencies on R
A, B, C, D: the attributes of R
AB: the set {A, B}
→: functionally determines: rows that agree on the left side agree on the right side
{ }: a set
In words: A and B together fix C, and C fixes D. In the options, C⁺ is the attribute closure of C.
```

options.text: (A, B, C) and (C, D); preserves all FDs
options.explanation: Correct. C fixes D but is not a superkey of the original. Split C with D into one part, and retain A, B and C in the other. Each original dependency has a local home, and both parts are in BCNF.

options.text: (A, B, C) and (B, C, D); preserves all FDs
options.explanation: This split is lossless, but the B/C/D part still has C fixing D without fixing B, so BCNF is not reached.

options.text: (A, B) and (C, D); preserves all FDs
options.explanation: The parts have no shared attributes, so arbitrary cross-combinations appear; the pair A and B fixing C is also not preserved.

options.text: The A/B/C part and the C/D part; loses the rule that the pair A and B fixes C
options.explanation: The dependency fixing C from the pair A and B fits in the A/B/C part and is preserved.

questions.workedExample:
1. Key of R: A and B are never on a right side, and their attribute closure is everything. Key AB.
2. For the rule fixing C from A together with B, that pair is a superkey. Fine.
3. For the rule fixing D from C, C is not a superkey. **Violation**, so split on C:

```formula
{A, B}⁺ = {A, B, C, D} = R
C⁺ = {C, D} ≠ R
R_1 = C⁺ ∩ R = CD
R_2 = C ∪ (R − C⁺) = ABC
where
{A, B}⁺, C⁺: attribute closures under F = {AB → C, C → D}
A, B, C, D: the attributes of R
AB: the set {A, B}
→: functionally determines
R: here, the set of all of R's attributes, ABCD
≠: is not equal to
R_1, R_2: the two parts of the split
CD, ABC, ABCD: sets of attributes written as letters side by side
∩: intersection; ∪: union; −: difference (of attribute sets)
{ }: a set
In words: C determines only C and D, so put C with D in one part and C with everything else in the other.
```

4. CD: key C. ABC: key AB, and a basis for the non-trivial projected FDs is the dependency from the pair A and B to C; implied augmentations and trivial FDs also hold. Both BCNF.
5. Preservation: AB → C in ABC, C → D in CD. **All preserved.**

questions.prompt:
Use 3NF synthesis on R(A, B, C, D, E) with the dependencies below. What is the result?

```formula
F = {A → B, C → D}
where
F: the set of functional dependencies on R
A, B, C, D, E: the attributes of R
→: functionally determines: rows that agree on the left side agree on the right side
{ }: a set
In words: A fixes B, and C fixes D. E is not mentioned by any FD.
```

options.text: (A, B) and (C, D)
options.explanation: Attribute E is missing altogether, and no part contains a key of R, so the join is lossy.

options.text: (A, B, C, D, E)
options.explanation: A fixes B while not being a superkey, and B is non-prime, so the original relation fails 3NF and must be decomposed.

options.text: (A, B), (C, D) and (E)
options.explanation: (E) holds E but shares no attributes with anything, so joining it is a Cartesian product. Step 3 adds a key relation, not leftover attributes.

options.text: (A, B), (C, D) and (A, C, E)
options.explanation: Correct. The cover gives AB and CD. The candidate key of R is ACE (A, C and E never appear on a right side), and no relation contains it, so add (A, C, E).

questions.workedExample:
1. The two original dependencies already form a singleton-right-side minimal FD cover.
2. One relation per left side: **AB**, **CD**.
3. Candidate key of R: A, C, E are never on a right side.

```formula
{A, C, E}⁺ = {A, B, C, D, E} = R
where
{A, C, E}⁺: the attribute closure of {A, C, E} under F = {A → B, C → D}
A, B, C, D, E: the attributes of R
→: functionally determines
R: here, the set of all of R's attributes
{ }: a set
In words: A brings B and C brings D, so A, C and E together reach everything: ACE is the key.
```

4. Neither AB nor CD contains ACE, so add **ACE**.
5. Nothing is a subset of another. Result: AB, CD, ACE. Lossless-join (the key relation ties everything together) and every FD is preserved.

questions.prompt: Which statements about decomposition algorithms are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: 3NF synthesis always produces a lossless-join, dependency-preserving decomposition
options.explanation: Correct. That guarantee is the reason to choose 3NF when BCNF would lose an FD.

options.text: BCNF decomposition always produces a lossless-join decomposition
options.explanation: Correct. Each split shares X, and X determines one whole part (X's attribute closure intersected with the relation), so the binary test passes at every step.

options.text: BCNF decomposition always preserves dependencies
options.explanation: False. The Teaching counterexample shows that a BCNF decomposition can lose dependency preservation. In the five-attribute example, the rule fixing E from C together with D is likewise not implied by the projected local FDs.

options.text: Every relation in BCNF is also in 3NF
options.explanation: Correct. BCNF's condition (left side a superkey) is stricter than 3NF's (left side a superkey *or* right side prime).

options.text: Every relation in 3NF is also in BCNF
options.explanation: False. Teaching is in 3NF but not BCNF, because 3NF allows a prime right side with a non-superkey left side.

questions.workedExample:
Summary of the guarantees:

| Algorithm | Lossless join | Preserves FDs |
|---|---|---|
| 3NF synthesis | always | always |
| BCNF decomposition | always | not always |

And the containment between the normal forms:

```formula
BCNF ⊂ 3NF ⊂ 2NF ⊂ 1NF
where
BCNF, 3NF, 2NF, 1NF: each stands for the set of all relations in that normal form
⊂: is a proper subset of: everything on the left is also on the right, and the right has more
In words: every BCNF relation is in 3NF, every 3NF relation in 2NF, and so on, but not the other way round.
```

lessons.title: Independent facts, 4NF and 5NF
lessons.summary: Independent facts, 4NF and 5NF, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
lessons.body:
## Beyond BCNF, briefly

BCNF removes redundancy caused by FDs, but not all redundancy. If an employee has a set of skills and, independently, a set of languages, storing `(emp, skill, language)` forces every skill to be paired with every language. That is a **multivalued dependency**: an employee determines a whole *set* of skills, independently of the other attributes.

```formula
emp ↠ skill
emp ↠ language
where
emp: the employee
skill: one of the employee's skills
language: one of the languages the employee speaks
↠: multivalued dependency (a double-headed arrow): the left side determines a set of values on the right, and that set does not depend on the remaining attributes
In words: an employee's skills and languages are two independent lists, so every combination ends up stored.
```

**4NF** splits it into `(emp, skill)` and `(emp, language)`. **5NF** handles join dependencies across three or more parts. Both are rare in practice, but the "independent facts in one table" smell is worth recognising.

## The exact condition matters

The dependency says more than “an employee can have several skills”. It requires all combinations of independently recorded skills and languages. Consider one employee with SQL and Python skills and English and French languages:

```
emp skill  language
 7  SQL    English
 7  SQL    French
 7  Python English
 7  Python French
```

There are four combinations. Recording only SQL/English and Python/French would say that the pairs are linked, not independent, and would violate the claimed multivalued dependency. Splitting the independent lists saves repetition while recovering those four rows by a natural join.

A multivalued dependency is trivial if its right attributes are already contained in the determinant, or the two sides together cover the whole heading. Fourth normal form requires a superkey determinant for every non-trivial multivalued dependency. Every FD implies an MVD, so this requirement also implies BCNF.

A **join dependency** says that a relation is always exactly the join of specified projections. Fifth normal form, also called project-join normal form, requires every non-trivial join dependency to follow from candidate-key rules. Three-way decompositions can matter even when no useful two-way split exists. Do not infer a join dependency merely because one sample happens to rejoin correctly: it must be a domain rule. Conversely, a supplier/part/project relation with no such rule must keep its three-way facts; splitting can invent combinations.

These are constraint-relative definitions. BCNF does not guarantee freedom from MVD redundancy, and 5NF does not promise that every application constraint or temporal fact is now represented correctly.

## Key takeaways

- Independent skill and language lists require all combinations in a combined table.
- 4NF controls non-trivial MVDs; 5NF controls join dependencies not implied by candidate keys.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [Fagin: multivalued dependencies and fourth normal form](https://research.ibm.com/publications/multivalued-dependencies-and-a-new-normal-form-for-relational-databases)
- [Fagin: Normal forms and relational database operators (1979)](https://research.ibm.com/publications/normal-forms-and-relational-database-operators)
- [Fagin: Domains and keys, section 5 definitions](https://s3.us.cloud-object-storage.appdomain.cloud/res-files/500-tods81.pdf)

questions.prompt: An employee has two skills and two languages. The business says the skill list and language list are independent. What must a flat employee/skill/language relation store for that employee?

options.text: Two rows pairing one skill with one language each
options.explanation: That records two specific pairs, so it cannot represent the required independent combinations.

options.text: Four rows, one for every skill and language combination
options.explanation: Correct. Independent lists require all four combinations. Splitting into employee/skill and employee/language relations removes that repetition and rejoins losslessly.

options.text: One row with arbitrary skill and language values
options.explanation: That loses the other values rather than modelling independent lists.

options.text: Four rows prove every possible employee relation is in 5NF
options.explanation: A sample does not establish the schema’s join dependencies, and four combinations do not by themselves prove 5NF.

questions.workedExample: For one employee, pair each of two skills with each of two languages: four combinations. Projecting the four rows onto employee/skill leaves two rows; projecting onto employee/language leaves two rows. Joining those projections on employee gives exactly the four original rows. The lossless split relies on the business rule that the lists are independent, rather than merely on today’s sample. A fifth-normal-form claim would additionally require examining all relevant join dependencies.

lessons.title: Measuring redundancy and copied values
lessons.summary: Measuring redundancy and copied values, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
lessons.body:
Normalisation stores every fact once, which makes writes simple and keeps the data consistent. The price is paid on reads: answering a question may require joining several tables.

**Denormalisation** is deliberately storing a fact more than once, or storing something derivable, so that reads get cheaper. It is not the absence of design. A denormalised schema starts from a normalised one and adds controlled redundancy, together with a plan for keeping the copies in agreement.

The rule of thumb: **normalise until it hurts, denormalise until it works**. And measure before you decide it hurts.

## First, check you actually need it

Joins on indexed keys can be efficient, but their cost depends on row counts, selectivity, caching and the selected join algorithm. A primary-key index can support selective lookups, but a join need not do one lookup per order: the planner may choose a hash, merge or nested-loop join. Cache state, selectivity and output size determine the measured cost. Teams often denormalise to fix a slow query whose real problem was something else. Before adding redundancy, try:

1. **An index** on the join or filter column. Missing indexes on foreign keys can slow selective joins or parent-row changes, since Postgres does not create them automatically.
2. **A covering index** (`CREATE INDEX ... INCLUDE (...)`) which can enable an index-only scan; PostgreSQL may still fetch heap pages for visibility checks.
3. **Fixing the query**: an N+1 loop in the application, a function on an indexed column, or fetching far more rows than needed.
4. **A cache** in front of the database, which is redundancy too but lives outside the schema.

If the read is still too slow, or is run so often that its cost dominates, denormalise.

## Copied current values and historical facts

Store a value from a parent row on its children, so a common read avoids a join:

```
orders(id, customer_id,
       customer_name,  -- copied
       total, ...)
```

Every change to `customer.name` must now also update that customer's orders. If one customer has 50,000 orders, a rename becomes a 50,000-row write.

> [!warning] Snapshot or cache?
> Ask whether the copy should follow the original. The shipping address *on an invoice* should **not** change when the customer moves: it is a historical fact about the order, and storing it is correct normalised design. A copy of the customer's *current* display name **should** follow the original: that is a cache, and true denormalisation. Confusing the two either changes history or leaves stale data.

## Key takeaways

- Measure the query and its plan before adding copied-value update fan-out.
- Historical snapshots model a different fact; a cached current value must follow its source.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL 18: refresh materialised views](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-refreshmaterializedview.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: generated columns](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-generated-columns.html)
- [AWS: transactional outbox](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/transactional-outbox.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: covering indexes and index-only scans](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-index-only-scans.html)

questions.prompt: An `invoice` table stores the customer's shipping address at the time of sale. A reviewer says it is "denormalised, because the address is already in `customer`" and wants it removed. What is the right response?

options.text: Agree; the invoice should join to `customer` for the address
options.explanation: Then old invoices would show the customer's new address after they move, altering historical records. The two addresses are different facts.

options.text: Keep it: the address on the invoice is a historical fact about that sale, not a copy of the current address, so storing it is correct normalised design
options.explanation: Correct. The invoice id determines the shipping address: that is its own functional dependency. It must not follow later changes to the customer, so it is not redundant.

options.text: Keep it, but add a trigger that updates it when the customer's address changes
options.explanation: That turns a historical record into a cache, which is exactly the bug to avoid: invoices would silently change.

options.text: Agree, and store the address only in the invoice instead
options.explanation: The customer's current address is a separate fact needed for future orders; it belongs on `customer` too.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ask: should this value change when the source changes?
2. Invoice shipping address: **no**. It records where that order went.
3. So it depends on the invoice, not on the customer's current state:

```formula
invoice_id → ship_address
where
invoice_id: the invoice's key
ship_address: the address the order was shipped to
→: functionally determines: each invoice has exactly one shipping address
In words: the address is a fact about this invoice, fixed when it was issued. It is a different fact from the customer's current address, not a duplicate of it.
```

4. A true denormalised copy would be something like `orders.customer_display_name`, meant to track the current name.

questions.prompt: A query joining `orders` to `customer` on orders.customer_id = customer.id is slow when fetching orders for a few customers. Assume customer.id is the primary key. A teammate proposes copying `customer.name` onto `orders` to avoid the join. In Postgres, what should you check first?

options.text: Whether `orders.customer_id` has an index, since Postgres does not create indexes on foreign-key columns automatically
options.explanation: Correct to investigate. PostgreSQL does not automatically index the referencing column. An index may help this selective lookup or parent deletes; confirm with EXPLAIN rather than assuming it fixes every slow join.

options.text: Whether `customer.id` has an index
options.explanation: A primary key always gets a unique index in Postgres, so this is already in place.

options.text: Whether the join should be rewritten as a subquery
options.explanation: An equivalent subquery usually gets the same plan. The access path, not the syntax, is the likely issue.

options.text: Nothing; joins are always slow, so denormalising is the standard fix
options.explanation: Indexed joins can be efficient, but cost depends on input sizes, selectivity, cache state and the chosen algorithm. Denormalising should follow measurement.

questions.workedExample:
1. PostgreSQL creates backing indexes for primary and unique constraints, but does not automatically index the referencing foreign-key columns.
2. Inspect `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on a safe read to see the actual plan and work. A sequential scan is not automatically a mistake; scanning much of a table can be appropriate.
3. For a selective customer lookup, test `CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id);`. Compare measured execution and write overhead.
4. Consider a copied name only after query and index fixes, with an explicit maintenance plan.

questions.prompt: In a chat app, `message` rows copy the sender's `display_name`. A user with 2,000,000 messages changes their display name, and the app updates all copies in one transaction. Which problem is most likely?

options.text: None; Postgres updates 2 million rows as cheaply as one
options.explanation: Each update creates a PostgreSQL row version and WAL; index work depends on whether a HOT update is possible. Millions of row updates can be costly even without new index entries.

options.text: The new name will be visible in some messages before others
options.explanation: Within one query snapshot on the primary, a transaction’s changes are observed atomically. Separate Read Committed statements can straddle the commit, and asynchronous replicas may still lag. A single transaction does not expose partially committed copies.

options.text: The transaction will violate a foreign key
options.explanation: Copying a name does not involve a foreign key; nothing references `display_name`.

options.text: A large, long transaction that writes millions of PostgreSQL row versions and substantial WAL, retains locks, can increase replica lag, and leaves obsolete versions to reclaim
options.explanation: Correct. Copied-value update fan-out is the price of copying a frequently changed value widely. Better: store `sender_id` and join, or treat old messages as historical snapshots that keep the old name.

questions.workedExample:
1. Rows touched: 2,000,000 messages, each a new PostgreSQL row version in Postgres's MVCC.
2. Each also writes WAL and, unless the update qualifies as a HOT update, new index entries.
3. Locks on all 2 million rows are held until commit; concurrent edits to those messages block.
4. Streaming replicas must replay all that WAL, so this can increase lag; the amount depends on replay capacity.
5. Lesson: denormalise values that are read a lot **and change rarely**. Display names change; `sender_id` does not, so join on it, or cache names outside the database.

lessons.title: Maintaining counters under writes
lessons.summary: Maintaining counters under writes, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
lessons.body:
## Counters and write contention

`post.comment_count` saves a `COUNT(*)` over comments on every page view. If a post page is read 1,000 times a second and gets 5 comments a second, you trade 1,000 counts for 5 increments.

A trigger keeps it in step within the same transaction:

```sql
CREATE FUNCTION bump_count()
RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
  UPDATE post
     SET comment_count = comment_count + 1
   -- Increment the parent for this comment.
   WHERE id = NEW.post_id;
  RETURN NEW;
END $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER comment_ins
AFTER INSERT ON comment
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION bump_count();
```

The fixture assumes `post.id` is a primary key, `comment.post_id` is a non-null foreign key, and `post.comment_count` is non-null and initialised to zero. Each inserted comment adds one; rolling back its transaction also rolls back the increment. A production implementation must cover deletion, moving a comment between posts, bulk maintenance and any path that bypasses ordinary row triggers, such as `TRUNCATE`. This insert-only example intentionally demonstrates drift when another event is omitted. The hidden cost is **contention**. Every comment on a viral post updates the same row, and each `UPDATE` holds that row's lock until its transaction commits, so writers queue behind one another. Remedies: split the counter into several rows (say 16) and sum them on read (sharded counters), or buffer increments and apply them in batches.

## Key takeaways

- A database counter update avoids a lost increment but makes one parent row a contention point.
- Cover every mutation event and reconcile stored counts with their source.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL 18: refresh materialised views](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-refreshmaterializedview.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: generated columns](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-generated-columns.html)
- [AWS: transactional outbox](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/transactional-outbox.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: row locks](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/explicit-locking.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: CREATE TRIGGER](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-createtrigger.html)

questions.prompt: A trigger increments `post.comment_count` on each comment insert. When a post goes viral, comment inserts on that post slow dramatically, while inserts on other posts are fine. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The `comment` table's index is fragmented
options.explanation: Fragmentation alone does not explain why inserts for one parent row queue while other parents are unaffected; the shared counter row is the direct contention point.

options.text: The trigger runs `COUNT(*)` on every insert
options.explanation: The trigger shown in the lesson increments; it does not count. The slowdown is specific to one post's row.

options.text: Every insert updates the same `post` row, and each transaction holds that row's lock until commit, so the inserts queue behind each other
options.explanation: Correct. A hot counter row serialises its writers. Shard the counter across N rows and sum on read, or buffer increments and apply them in batches.

options.text: Postgres limits each table to one trigger execution at a time
options.explanation: Triggers run in each transaction concurrently. The bottleneck is the row lock, not the trigger mechanism.

questions.workedExample:
1. `UPDATE post SET comment_count = comment_count + 1 WHERE id = 42` takes a row-level lock on post 42.
2. The lock is held until the inserting transaction commits.
3. Concurrent comment inserts on post 42 must wait for each other: throughput on that post drops to one transaction at a time.
4. Sharded counter:

Illustrative design, not executable SQL:

```text
post_counter(post_id, shard, n)
write: choose one of sixteen shard rows
read: sum n for the requested post
```

Sixteen rows provide up to sixteen distinct row-lock targets. Random choices still collide, and actual throughput is bounded by transaction duration and other shared work; this is not a promise of sixteenfold speed.

link.title: PostgreSQL 18: row-level locking

questions.prompt: `post.comment_count` is maintained by an `AFTER INSERT` trigger only. Moderators delete spam comments directly in the database. Six months later, which symptom do you expect, and how do you find affected posts?

options.text: Counts are too low; find them with `WHERE comment_count < 0`
options.explanation: Deletes do not decrement anything, so counts only ever go up. They will be too high, never negative.

options.text: Counts are too high; compare the counter with the real count, for example `WHERE p.comment_count <> (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM comment c WHERE c.post_id = p.id)`
options.explanation: Correct. Every deleted comment leaves the counter one too high. A reconciliation query comparing the copy with its source finds the drift; then add an `AFTER DELETE` trigger and backfill.

options.text: Counts are correct, because Postgres runs `AFTER INSERT` triggers in reverse on delete
options.explanation: There is no such reversal. A trigger fires only for its declared events; one PostgreSQL trigger can handle several events if its function handles each correctly. An INSERT-only trigger does not run on DELETE.

options.text: The deletes fail, because the trigger depends on the comments
options.explanation: An insert trigger does not stop deletes. The deletes succeed and the counter silently drifts.

questions.workedExample:
1. Inserts add 1; deletes change nothing:

```formula
c_stored = N_ins
c_real = N_ins − N_del
c_stored ≥ c_real
where
c_stored: the value in post.comment_count
N_ins: committed comment insertions since the counter was correctly initialised to zero; assume no moves between posts
N_del: committed comment deletions in that same interval
c_real: the true number of comments, COUNT(*)
≥: is greater than or equal to
In words: the stored count is too high by exactly the number of deleted comments.
```
2. Reconcile:

```sql
SELECT p.id, p.comment_count,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM comment c
   WHERE c.post_id = p.id) AS real
FROM post p
WHERE p.comment_count <> (
  SELECT COUNT(*) FROM comment c
  WHERE c.post_id = p.id);
```

3. Fix the cause (an `AFTER DELETE` trigger, and handle `UPDATE` of `post_id`), then backfill with an `UPDATE` from the real counts.
4. Keep the reconciliation as a scheduled check, because manual fixes and restores cause drift too.

lessons.title: Materialised results and generated values
lessons.summary: Materialised results and generated values, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
lessons.body:
## Materialised views

Reports such as daily sales per product scan millions of rows. Precompute them:

```sql
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_sales AS
SELECT o.day, l.product_id,
       SUM(l.qty * l.price_paid) AS revenue
FROM orders o JOIN line l
  ON l.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY o.day, l.product_id;

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX
  ON daily_sales (day, product_id);

REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW
  CONCURRENTLY daily_sales;
```

In Postgres, a materialised view is a stored query result. It does not update itself; `REFRESH` re-runs the whole query. Plain `REFRESH` locks out readers while it runs; concurrent refresh lets ordinary reads continue. Concurrent refresh requires an already-populated view and a qualifying unique index on plain columns covering every row, without a partial predicate or expression. Only one refresh can run on a given view at a time. Relative speed depends on how much changed, so it is not correct to promise that concurrent refresh is always slower. Core Postgres has no incremental refresh (extensions such as `pg_ivm` add it), whereas Oracle's fast-refresh materialised views and SQL Server's indexed views maintain results incrementally, with restrictions on the query shape.

The view is as stale as its last refresh. That suits a dashboard refreshed every 15 minutes; it does not suit a stock level shown at checkout.

## Generated same-row values

A value computed from other columns *in the same row* is the cheapest kind, because there is no fan-out. Postgres generated columns do it declaratively:

```sql
ALTER TABLE line ADD COLUMN amount
  NUMERIC GENERATED ALWAYS AS
  (qty * price_paid) STORED;
```

`STORED` computes on write and can be indexed. PostgreSQL 16–17 support the stored kind. PostgreSQL 18 also supports `VIRTUAL`, the default when the kind is omitted, computed on read. Explicit `STORED` makes this example portable across those versions. Generation expressions must use allowed immutable expressions over the current row: no subqueries, aggregates, other rows or other generated columns. PostgreSQL 18 imposes extra built-in-type/function restrictions on virtual expressions.

The SQL assumes `orders(id, day)` and `line(order_id, product_id, qty, price_paid)`, with quantity an integer and price an exact numeric amount in pounds per item. Multiplying gives pounds for the line; summing gives pounds for that day and product. These are example fixtures, not assumptions that every shop has one timezone or one currency. A materialised view is a stored snapshot from the query’s read snapshot; it is not guaranteed to include writes that commit during its refresh.

## Key takeaways

- PostgreSQL materialised views stay unchanged until refreshed.
- Concurrent refresh needs a populated view and a qualifying unique index; generated values have stricter same-row rules.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL 18: refresh materialised views](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-refreshmaterializedview.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: generated columns](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-generated-columns.html)
- [AWS: transactional outbox](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/transactional-outbox.html)

questions.prompt: You create `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_sales AS SELECT ...` in Postgres at 09:00. New orders arrive all morning. What does `SELECT * FROM daily_sales` show at 11:00?

options.text: An error, because the view is stale
options.explanation: Stale data is returned without warning; Postgres does not track staleness for you.

options.text: Live results, because a view always re-runs its query
options.explanation: That describes an ordinary view. A *materialised view* stores the result instead of re-running the query.

options.text: Results updated incrementally after each new order
options.explanation: Some databases offer this (Oracle fast refresh, SQL Server indexed views), but core Postgres does not.

options.text: The results as of 09:00, because a materialised view stores its result and changes only when you run `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW`
options.explanation: Correct. It is a snapshot. Core Postgres never refreshes it automatically or incrementally.

questions.workedExample:
1. `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` runs the query once and stores the rows.
2. Later inserts into the base tables do not touch it.
3. `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_sales` re-runs the entire query and replaces the contents.
4. So at 11:00 you see the 09:00 data. Schedule refreshes (for example with `pg_cron`) at whatever staleness the report can tolerate.
